detail.abstract: Osteoporosis is a progressive skeletal disease characterised by decreased bone mass and deterioration of bone microarchitecture, ultimately leading to fractures and long-term disability. Early diagnosis remains challenging because the disease is clinically silent until fracture occurs. Conventional diagnostic tools, particularly dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry (DEXA), are expensive, equipment-intensive, and inaccessible in resource-limited settings. To address these limitations, this study proposes a multimodal deep learning framework that integrates knee X-ray imaging with structured patient clinical data for early osteoporosis detection. The framework combines Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) and Vision Transformers (ViTs) for imaging feature extraction and incorporates clinical variables , including age, sex, bone mineral density history, previous fractures, and lifestyle markers , through multimodal fusion mechanisms. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed multimodal fusion model achieved an accuracy of 93.6%, precision of 92.8%, recall of 93.1%, and AUC of 0.96, outperforming both CNN-only (accuracy: 86.4%) and ViT-only (accuracy: 88.2%) baseline models. Explainable AI techniques including Grad-CAM, transformer attention maps, and SHAP analysis were integrated to enhance clinical interpretability. These findings demonstrate the significant potential of multimodal AI frameworks for accessible, cost-effective, and clinically trustworthy osteoporosis screening.

title: Respiratory Health Effects of Household and Ambient Air Pollution in Sub-Saharan Africa: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis

detail.title: Respiratory Health Effects of Household and Ambient Air Pollution in Sub-Saharan Africa: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis

detail.abstract:
Background: Sub-Saharan Africa (sSA) bears a disproportionately high burden of household air pollution (HAP) and rising ambient air pollution (AAP), yet regional evidence on their health impacts remains limited or fragmented. We systematically reviewed and meta-analyzed all the studies examining associations between HAP/AAP exposures and respiratory health outcomes in sSA.

Methods: We conducted systematic search in four databases (PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science and Google Scholar) through December 2025. We included peer-reviewed cohort, case-control, and panel studies assessing associations of respiratory outcomes with objectively measured HAP/AAP exposures/standardized WHO clinical assessment for case-control studies. Risk of bias was assessed using a modified Newcastle–Ottawa Scale. Meta-analyses used DerSimonian–Laird random-effects models with prespecified subgroup analyses. The protocol was pre-registered with PROSPERO (CRD420251064034).

Findings: Of 4,510 records, 14 studies from nine sSA countries met the inclusion criteria (11 eligible for meta-analysis). Summary effect estimates (EE) showed an overall 30% increased risk of adverse respiratory outcomes from household and AAP exposure (summary EE (95% CI)) = 1.30 (1.16–1.45)). Subgroup analyses revealed stronger effects for symptoms of cough, wheeze, phlegm, EE = 2.01 (1.10–3.66) than for respiratory infections, including pneumonia, EE = 1.22 (1.07-1.39). The adverse effects were more pronounced for children under 5 years, EE = 1.39 (1.20–1.62). Notably, prenatal exposure was linked to a 23% higher risk of infant respiratory infections, EE = 1.23 (1.07–1.41). Use of polluting fuel, such as firewood or charcoal, was associated with about 3 times higher risks of developing an adverse respiratory outcome, EE= 2.81 (1.95-4.29). High heterogeneity (I2 = 85.7% for overall analysis) reflected diverse geographic settings and variations in exposure-outcome assessment methods.

Interpretation: This systematic review and meta-analysis provide compelling evidence that both household and AAP exposure increase the risk of adverse respiratory outcomes in sSA, especially among children under 5 years. Interventions targeting clean household energy, improved ventilation, and ambient air quality regulation can lead to great environmental and health co-benefits. This systematic review also underscores key evidence gaps in harmonized exposure assessment and longitudinal evaluations of independent and joint HAP–AAP effects. Future multicountry cohort studies with standardized exposure metrics are needed to strengthen causal inference and guide targeted mitigation strategies in the region.

title: Effect of Artificial Intelligence on GDP Growth and Inflation A System Dynamics Approach of the AI-Driven Economy 2020-2060

detail.title: Effect of Artificial Intelligence on GDP Growth and Inflation A System Dynamics Approach of the AI-Driven Economy 2020-2060

detail.abstract: We develop and simulate a System Dynamics (SD) model to study the macroeconomic effects of large-scale Artificial Intelligence (AI) adoption on inflation and economic growth over the period 2020-2060. The model captures three interlocking subsystems, capital accumulation, labour-market transition, and price-level dynamics through seven stocks, eleven flows, and four feedback loops calibrated to 2020 global baselines. The baseline simulation reveals a robust two-phase narrative: a deflationary transition shock (2020-2040) driven by rapid routine-worker displacement outpacing reskilling, followed by a productivity-led stabilisation Verma & Reddy (2026) Working Paper (2040-2060) in which augmented-workforce growth pushes the GDP index toward 3× by 2060 and settles inflation near 3.0-3.5%. Sensitivity analysis over the AI productivity multiplier (κ) shows non-linear leverage: doubling κ roughly quadruples long-run GDP. Sensitivity analysis of the novel-task absorption rate reveals strong nonlinearities, moderate labour reabsorption stabilises the transition, while excessive absorption into low-productivity AI-era gig and microtask employment suppresses long-run growth despite reducing unemployment. A reskilling-efficiency policy experiment demonstrates that tripling efficiency from 0.05 to 0.33 yr-1 boosts long-run growth by approx 400 bp while compressing the transition-shock window by roughly a decade. The analysis highlights the reskilling lag as the central bottleneck for beneficial AI diffusion and provides quantitative grounding for policy design.

detail.title: Optional Stopping and the Look-Elsewhere Effect in Bayesian Inference

publicationDetails.detailsText: This paper has not appeared in any paper series, journal, or book, and has not been accepted for publication. It is being prepared for journal submission.

detail.abstract: The look-elsewhere effect (LEE) and the broader machinery of selection-bias correction are routine in frequentist data analysis but contested in Bayesian practice. We make three points for the applied analyst. First, when the auxiliary mechanism that drives selection is conditionally independent of the parameter given the observed data, it cancels from the Bayes factor; the work that the LEE performs in frequentist analyses is absorbed into the prior over candidate models or locations rather than added as a separate correction. Second, this cancellation is one instance of the same factorization that delivers stopping-rule irrelevance and randomization-irrelevance. Third, controlling for selection is therefore a likelihood-modeling decision, not a logical adjustment, and it is necessary to keep apart three quantities: the local Bayes factor at the selected location, the marginal Bayes factor for "anomaly somewhere," and the posterior probability that the selected location is the anomalous one. We illustrate with two cases run side by side: the 2012 Higgs boson search and the 2023 Kramnik-Nakamura chess dispute.

detail.title: Parsimonious Mixed Bergomi Models for Joint Calibration of VIX Futures and Options
detail.abstract: We propose a data-driven approach to reduce the mixed Bergomi model parameters. Our approach involves replacing the term structures of maturity-dependent parameters with simple parametric functional forms derived from calibrating VIX futures and options. Despite their simplicity, the proposed models are nearly as accurate as their classical counterparts in calibrating VIX futures and options, while improving interpretability. Additionally, empirical results demonstrate that the parsimonious models exhibit more stable parameter behaviour over time, making them more suitable for dynamic applications such as hedging.

title: Macro financial Insights on Nonperforming Loan in Nepal: Evidence from Econometrics and Machine Learning Algorithm

detail.title: Macro financial Insights on Nonperforming Loan in Nepal: Evidence from Econometrics and Machine Learning Algorithm
detail.abstract: This paper investigates the relationship of selected macroeconomic variables and bank-specific controls on nonperforming loans (NPL) of Nepalse commercial banks, using panel data spanning 2011Q1 to 2024Q4. It employs a dual approach, integrating random effects and fixed effects econometric estimation with machine learning regressions. Our analysis suggests that random forest is the preferred model over decision tree and XGBoost, and revealed that institutional features are relatively dominant over macroeconomic variables to explain the NPL. The lag NPL has highest importance (0.5650) followed by Credit to deposit ratio (0.2287), Return on equity (0.0559), NEPSE (0.0369), Interest margin (0.0267), Assets of the bank (0.0196), Export to import ratio (0.0124), Inflation (0.0107) and so on. Likewise, econometric estimate indicates that macroeconomic indicators such as NEPSE index, Remittance, and Money supply have a statistically significant relationship with NPL, whereas inflation, export-to-import ratio, exchange rate and GDP are statistically insignificant. In addition, bank specific controls such as past NPL, Credit to deposit ratio, Ownership, Asset size and Return on assets are significant. Surprisingly, the COVID-19 dummy is associated with a decline in NPL, reflecting the short-run effect of monetary and fiscal stimulus. Further, favorable macroeconomic environment helps to improve the asset quality of banks. Overall, NPL in Nepalese banks is largely explained by bank-specific variables supporting for bad management hypothesis whereas some macroeconomic indicators exhibits significant relationships referring some bad luck.

detail.abstract: Background: Weak D antigen is a variant of the RhD antigen with important implications for blood transfusion and maternal-fetal compatibility. Detecting weak D is essential for transfusion management because it influences the selection of blood components for RhD-negative individuals. This study aimed to assess the prevalence of weak D among 150 RhD-negative blood samples using the Du method in Shendi, Sudan, and to compare the findings with similar studies conducted worldwide. Methods: This cross-sectional descriptive study was conducted in Shendi, Sudan, to evaluate the presence of weak D in 150 RhD-negative blood samples. The Du method was used to detect weak D antigen, and the collected data were analyzed using SPSS software to determine statistical significance. Results: No cases of weak D were detected among the 150 samples tested using the Du method. The findings were compared with studies conducted in India, Poland, and other regions, which reported varying prevalence rates of weak D. The absence of weak D in the current study may reflect regional variations, differences in diagnostic techniques, or sample-specific factors. Conclusion: The study found no occurrence of weak D among the tested samples, highlighting the need for further research to investigate regional differences in weak D prevalence and the sensitivity of the Du method. These findings suggest that weak D may be rare in Shendi, Sudan; however, larger and more comprehensive studies are recommended to confirm these results and to evaluate their implications for transfusion practices.

title: The Implementability of Settlement: Pretrial Bargaining under Procedural Constraints

detail.title: The Implementability of Settlement: Pretrial Bargaining under Procedural Constraints
detail.abstract: Civil settlement is usually studied by taking the bargaining protocol and information structure as primitives. This paper treats the protocol itself as a legal object and studies how court-managed timing changes the equilibrium settlement correspondence. Court-managed scheduling, disclosure, discovery, and settlement conferences determine which information-producing histories are available before bargaining. The central question is whether a payoff-feasible settlement is also protocol-implementable. The main model compares discovery before bargaining with settlement bargaining before discovery. Holding trial values, litigation costs, and the prior fixed, changing only the order of discovery and bargaining changes the set of equilibrium-implementable settlements. In a two-type litigation environment, each type has a mutually beneficial settlement under full information. Under settlement-before-discovery, however, low-type settlement is implementable if and only if Ω = π(x H-x L)-(1-π)(c P + c D) ≤ 0. If Ω > 0, early bargaining induces screening and some payoff-feasible settlements fail; if Ω ≤ 0, early bargaining induces pooling and avoids discovery delay. Thus procedural timing has a threshold-dependent dual effect. Extensions show how delay leverage and court-managed communication fit the same feasible-history framework.

title: High-Yield Savings Accounts vs. Series I Bonds: Which Is Better for Beating Inflation?
affiliations: Marquette University

detail.title: High-Yield Savings Accounts vs. Series I Bonds: Which Is Better for Beating Inflation?
detail.abstract: This study compares Series I Savings Bonds and High-Yield Savings Accounts as inflation hedging vehicles for retail investors. Using monthly data from June 1999 through April 2026 (310 months), I derive I Bond composite rates directly from Consumer Price Index data and construct a HYSA proxy based on the 1 Year Treasury rate minus a 0.5% spread. The historical analysis reveals that I Bonds delivered an average annualized real return of positive 0.83% over the 27 year sample period, while HYSAs delivered a negative 0.91% real return. A $10,000 investment in I Bonds in June 1999 would have grown to $12,363 in real purchasing power by April 2026. The same investment in a HYSA would have declined to $7,884, a difference of $4,479 in favor of I Bonds. I Bonds beat inflation in 77.1% of months, compared to just 31.9% for HYSAs. Forward looking scenario analysis under 2%, 3.5%, and 5% CPI assumptions projects that I Bonds will continue to outperform HYSAs by approximately 0.40 percentage points annually over the next five years. I conclude that for investors with a holding period of at least one year, I Bonds offer a superior structural hedge against inflation compared to HYSAs. The $10,000 annual purchase limit remains the primary constraint for larger portfolios.

detail.abstract: Kentucky faces significant health care professional shortages, particularly in its rural and Appalachian areas. In 2023, metropolitan counties in Kentucky had approximately 37 physicians per 10,000 population, while Nonmetropolitan counties had only 12. Trends among Kentucky's rural physicians have been to move away from independent practice, as independent physicians and independent rural practices in Kentucky have dropped by 42 and 39 percent, respectively, since 2019. Shortages of health care professionals in Kentucky extend beyond physicians to dentists, audiologists, mental health professionals, and more. The literature on health care professional location decisions indicates that location of upbringing and of training have outsized impacts on where a professional elects to practice. Additional influences include scholarship provision, student loan repayment, and expanded practice authority. Internationally trained professionals can assist in providing care in shortage areas, but their recruitment in Kentucky is limited by federal immigration policy. Currently, Kentucky has two loan repayment programs, a health care professional scholarship program, and a health care careers educational outreach program. Each of these provides elements the literature suggests are beneficial to at least modestly increasing the supply of health care professionals, but with limitations. A theme among them tends to be a lack of support for those who would like to enter independent practice. Kentucky should coordinate and expand its collective programs to increase early interest in health care professional education and the scholarship and loan repayment opportunities that exist to make such education more affordable. Reorienting state programs to encourage independent and solo practice would likely also be beneficial to health care access in rural areas of Kentucky.

title: Don't Draw the Downs Apart -How to Best Simulate Asset Price Drawdowns
affiliations: University of Hamburg, University of Hamburg, University of Hamburg and University of Mannheim - Department of International Finance

detail.title: Don't Draw the Downs Apart -How to Best Simulate Asset Price Drawdowns
detail.abstract: This paper evaluates bootstrap simulation techniques for calculating the distribution of maximum drawdown (MDD), an important risk indicator in the stock and cryptocurrency markets. Using stochastic dominance tests, we assess the full distributional properties of the MDD under different methods. Our findings reveal that the standard Efron (1979) bootstrap, which assumes independence and identically distributed random variables, systematically underestimates the true MDD. While the moving block bootstrap provides reasonable estimates, it is subject to non-stationarity bias, particularly when large drawdowns occur at the boundaries of a return series. Alternative procedures, such as block-block bootstrap, tapered bootstrap and robust resampling, do not lead to better results. Of all the methods studied, the stationary bootstrap of Politis and Romano (1994) produces the most accurate and robust results, particularly for longer block lengths.

detail.abstract:
Background. The ethical dimensions of autonomous AI decision-making have moved from speculative concern to operational reality as AI systems are deployed in healthcare diagnosis, defence targeting, criminal justice risk assessment, and adjacent high-stakes domains. The philosophical literature on moral agency, value alignment, and accountability attribution has produced a substantial body of analysis, yet translating this analysis into operational governance practice remains uneven. The responsibility gap, the value-alignment problem, and the question of human dignity in automated decisions together define the ethical terrain practitioners must navigate.

Purpose. This paper synthesises the philosophical and applied ethics literature on autonomous decision-making in high-stakes domains, examining moral agency and accountability attribution, the structural features of the value alignment problem, the ethical implications of AI deployment in healthcare, defence, and criminal justice, the requirements of human dignity and the right to human review, and the translation of philosophical principles into operational practitioner ethics frameworks.

Approach. The paper adopts a narrative literature review methodology drawing on authoritative sources spanning analytical moral philosophy (Vallor and Vierkant, 2024; Sparrow, 2021; Hakli and Mäkelä, 2019), value alignment research (Russell, 2019; Gabriel, 2020; Hadfield-Menell et al., 2016; Krakovna et al., 2020), domain-specific ethics literature in healthcare, defence, and criminal justice, and emerging operational guidance including UNESCO's Recommendation on the Ethics of Artificial Intelligence.

Findings. Three findings are advanced. First, the responsibility gap arises not solely from epistemic and control failures of AI systems but from structural failures to embed reciprocal moral relations of mutual vulnerability between agents and patients within governance practice (Vallor and Vierkant, 2024). Second, the value alignment problem is not a technical problem with a forthcoming technical solution but a structural feature of optimisation under value uncertainty, requiring governance treatment rather than purely technical resolution. Third, translating philosophical principles into operational ethics frameworks is the central practitioner-scholar challenge of the period, with the gap between abstract principles and applied controls remaining the dominant source of ethical failure in deployed AI.

Implications. Practitioners deploying AI in high-stakes domains require ethics frameworks that integrate moral philosophy, applied ethics, and operational governance. The paper proposes that operational ethics for AI is best understood as a discipline that bridges the principles articulated in instruments such as UNESCO's Recommendation, the UAE AI Charter, and the EU AI Act with the management system documentation, control implementation, and assurance practices of regulated deployment.

title: Investor Patience, Capital Gains Overhang, and Stock Mispricing
affiliations: The University of Hong Kong - Faculty of Business and Economics and Shenzhen University

detail.title: Investor Patience, Capital Gains Overhang, and Stock Mispricing
detail.abstract: This paper examines the role of investor patience in stock mispricing by adopting capital gains overhang to capture relative mispricing. We first show that capital gains overhang is overall positively priced worldwide, but with a substantial variation. We then show that past losers (i.e., stocks with paper capital losses) have lower future returns in patient countries than in impatient countries. In contrast, past winners (i.e., stocks with paper capital gains) do not have significantly higher future returns in patient countries. The role of patience remains robust after controlling for various well-known country-level variables, highlighting its underexplored role in the literature.

title: Restructuring Cosmetology TVET and Establishing a Centre of Excellence in Kenya: A Technical Framework with Lessons from the Greening of the Level 6 Curriculum

detail.title: Restructuring Cosmetology TVET and Establishing a Centre of Excellence in Kenya: A Technical Framework with Lessons from the Greening of the Level 6 Curriculum
detail.abstract: The greening and digitization of Kenya's Level 6 Cosmetology curriculum revealed persistent structural and scientific gaps. This paper proposes a technical framework for restructuring cosmetology TVET and establishing a Centre of Excellence (CoE). The framework is aligned with the Kenya National Qualifications Framework (KNQF) and informed by global best practices. Key elements include a stackable, modular pathway from KNQF Level 4 (Certificate) to Level 7 (Higher National Diploma) with two distinct progression routes-Beauty Therapy (service focus) and Cosmetology (scientific focus); mandatory applied sciences (microbiology, trichology, dermatology, cosmetic chemistry, nutrition, lab techniques, holistic wellness); a formulation laboratory; Recognition of Prior Learning (RPL) as a mapping tool; upstream circular economy (UCE) and bioeconomy principles embedded at every training level; a graduate tracer study system; KEBS standardization; and a documented guide for other TVET institutions (the Circular Cosmetology TVET Playbook). The paper also highlights the need to upskill existing TVET trainers through a cascade model that draws on internal field experts and cross-departmental collaboration. It calls for a mandatory gap analysis before any institution implements the framework and proposes a small technical working group to oversee curriculum review. The paper concludes with an open invitation to development partners, TVET institutions, private sector actors, and policymakers to collaborate in piloting and scaling the model. The author welcomes critique and suggestions from industry experts and thought leaders.

title: Empirical Research on ESG Factor-Optimized Asset Pricing and Multifactor Models
affiliations: , University College Dublin (UCD) - Michael Smurfit Graduate School of Business and University College Dublin

detail.title: Empirical Research on ESG Factor-Optimized Asset Pricing and Multifactor Models
detail.abstract: Despite their increasing importance in worldwide investment plans and the key role played by the Chinese economy in the green transition worldwide, the asset pricing role of Environmental, Social, and Governance (ESG) factors in Chinese asset markets and the implications for optimal portfolio management are still understudied. This work addresses this gap by constructing an ESG-factor-mimicking portfolio and adding it as a risk factor to the traditional Fama-French three-factor model, thereby creating a four-factor risk factor pricing model for the Chinese stock market. We systematically investigate the explanatory ability of the model by building size-value and size-ESG investment portfolios. Including the ESG factor not only improves the model's capacity to account for cross-sectional variation in stock returns but also helps expose notable sector-specific effects, especially in sectors where ESG issues are most relevant.

title: From CEO to (She)EO: Gender Transitions in Executive Leadership and Firm Dynamics

detail.title: From CEO to (She)EO: Gender Transitions in Executive Leadership and Firm Dynamics
detail.abstract: This paper studies whether the appointment of a female CEO in previously male led firms affects firm performance and the treatment of female talent. Using administrative employer employee and firm tax records from Costa Rica, I compare firms that replace a male CEO with a female CEO to firms that replace a male CEO with another male CEO. The design combines entropy weighting on pre transition characteristics and outcome histories with dynamic event study specifications around CEO succession. I find no evidence that male to female transitions change firm scale, as measured by revenue, value added, assets, or employment. Instead, these transitions are followed by higher value added per worker, revenue per worker, profit margins, total factor productivity, and survival probabilities. These gains coincide with higher female employment, higher quality female hires, and narrower within firm gender wage gaps. At the same time, incoming female CEOs are paid substantially less than comparable male successors. The evidence suggests that CEO gender transitions affect firm outcomes partly through changes in how female talent is recruited, represented, and compensated.

detail.abstract: This paper analyzes Sweden's entrepreneurial performance from an institutional and evolutionary perspective, using the concept of the collaborative innovation bloc. It argues that economic development is driven not by entrepreneurial entry per se, but by the capacity of institutional arrangements to channel entrepreneurial effort into large-scale, productivity-enhancing activities. Sweden provides an instructive case: despite strong performance in innovation and start-up formation, the economy performs less well in turning young firms into globally competitive enterprises. The analysis emphasizes the complementarity between entrepreneurs and key actors-investors, skilled employees, and competent customers-and the role of institutional incentives in coordinating their interaction over time. While past reforms have improved conditions for entry, remaining distortions in taxation, labor market regulation, and capital allocation may bias outcomes toward early exit rather than sustained growth.

detail.abstract: Rising temperatures may influence everyday food choices in ways that have important implications for nutrition and public health. This paper studies how short-run exposure to extreme temperatures affects the composition of household grocery purchases in the United States. Using a nationally representative household panel dataset of grocery transactions merged with local weather information, we exploit within-household variation and estimate two-way fixed effects models to identify causal effects. We find that hotter weeks consistently shift food purchases toward less healthy items and reduce overall diet quality, with little change in total grocery spending. In contrast, unusually cold weeks lead to slight increases in total spending but do not significantly alter the nutritional composition of purchases. These results suggest that heat exposure primarily induces households to reallocate spending toward less healthy foods rather than to change how much they spend, whereas cold exposure mainly affects the volume of groceries purchased. The heat-induced effects on healthiness of food purchases are modest in the short run but are highly robust and more pronounced for households with less healthy baseline purchasing patterns. These findings highlight an underexplored channel through which rising temperatures may degrade diet quality, underscoring the potential public health and welfare costs of climate change.

detail.abstract: We study the use of objective and subjective performance evaluations in the provision of incentives, with a particular focus on how the timing of subjective performance evaluation affects its role in the cost-minimizing contract. We show that early reporting not only increases reliance on subjective performance evaluation but also increases the likelihood that the optimal contract involves no third-party payments. We derive conditions under which subjective performance evaluation is used, and relate it to the incentive role and confirmatory role of accounting information. Regarding the properties of the performance measures, we find that under early reporting, positive bias in both subjective and objective performance measurement promotes the use of subjective performance evaluation.

title: Machine Behavior in Multi-Unit Auctions
affiliations: University of Houston - Department of Decision & Information Sciences, Beijing Normal University (BNU) - School of Systems Science and UNSW Business School

detail.title: Machine Behavior in Multi-Unit Auctions
detail.abstract: Multi-unit auctions are central to markets such as electricity, carbon emissions, and government securities, yet much of their theoretical analysis relies on static, single-shot models that fail to capture strategic adaptation and learning in repeated interactions. As algorithmic bidding becomes increasingly prevalent, understanding the endogenous bidding strategies that emerge through repeated interaction is critical. To address this gap, we develop a deep reinforcement learning framework using Deep Q-Networks, in which autonomous agents learn to bid through extensive self-play in simulated multi-unit auction environments with repeated interactions. Employing a 2 × 2 experimental design, we systematically vary both the cost structure (standard "high-cost" environments versus "low-cost" settings with a substantial share of zero-cost bidders) and auction format (single-unit vs. multi-unit). After more than 80 million training iterations, we find that, as the proportion of zero-cost bidders increases, such as those representing renewable resources in electricity markets, both average bids and clearing prices decrease overall. Moreover, contrary to standard intuition, multi-unit auctions induce lower individual bids than single-unit auctions because agents with low private costs aggressively bid low or even negative values to increase their chance of winning while relying on other winners to set higher clearing prices. Although average bids are lower, multi-unit auctions generate higher clearing prices driven by the order-statistics effects under the uniform-price mechanism. Interestingly, negative bids and clearing prices emerge endogenously exclusively in multi-unit settings.

detail.abstract:
This paper studies advertising competition when consumers rely on associative
memory. Memory is modeled as a network in which brands become linked to valuerelevant
concepts through repeated exposure, and advertising operates by triggering
recall. In this environment, communication shapes consideration sets by determining
which brands and attributes are jointly brought to mind. In contrast to belief-based
persuasion models, communication in our setting is effective even when it conveys little
or no new information, as long as it succeeds in inducing recall of the brand together
with a value-relevant concept.
The paper shows that firms face a trade-off when emphasizing product benefits. Associating
a brand with value is necessary to encourage consideration, but doing so may
also activate competing brands through shared memory links, intensifying competition.
As a result, firms may optimally rely on uninformative advertising: once associations
are established, simple brand reminders can sustain relevance while limiting competitive
spillovers. When advertising effectiveness is intermediate, however, firms are forced to
emphasize value, leading to joint recall and heightened competition. As a result, firms’
profits depend non-monotonically on advertising effectiveness.
We further show that utility-irrelevant associations – such as colors, mascots, or
symbols – may allow firms to circumvent this trade-off: By linking these cues to value
during earlier communication, firms can later use them to trigger recall without activating
competing brands, thereby softening competition and increasing profits.

title: Electrifying Bike-share Systems at Scale
affiliations: Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) - Sloan School of Management,  and Rotman School of Management

detail.title: Electrifying Bike-share Systems at Scale
detail.abstract: Bike-share electrification is accelerating globally. Cities primarily rely on manual battery swapping but are increasingly considering in-station charging as an alternative to power the fleet. Using real-world data from Manhattan, we develop an optimization methodology that coordinates in-station charging and battery swapping, while accounting for network effects and endogenous demand. The resulting model is a large-scale mixed-integer nonlinear program, integrating over 10,000 discrete choice models to capture city-wide demand patterns. We develop a machine-learning-augmented approach for this class of problems, using ReLU neural networks to construct compact mixed-integer linear programming surrogates of the nonlinear model. Theoretical results suggest a tradeoff between computational tractability and solution quality, parametrized by the number of positive vs. nonpositive weights in the neural network. We use these results to design solution algorithms based on tailored neural networks, feature transformations, and a dual-informed decision-aware policy. This method yields provably high-quality solutions to otherwise intractable problem instances at practical scales. From a practical standpoint, we find that electrifying 20% of stations in Manhattan can reduce battery swapping by 80% without sacrificing ridership, and can even eliminate the need for battery swapping upon improvements in e-bike technologies. Moreover, our results suggest that electrification is most effective in areas with high traffic, long e-bike downtime, and strong connections to high-demand regions.

title: Essays on Industrial Organization

detail.title: Essays on Industrial Organization
detail.abstract: Endogenous Product Choices and Optimal Regulations: A Case of E-Cigarettes This paper studies firms’ endogenous product-entry decisions in the U.S. e-cigarette market by combining a random-coefficients logit demand model with a multi-stage model of product entry. Big firms first choose which nicotine categories to serve; small firms then make ordered entry decisions in response. This structure generates a unique equilibrium prediction for the number of small-firm entrants in each product category and partially identifies fixed costs for big firms. Competition effects are heterogeneous: big-firm presence depresses small-firm profitability while small firms depress each other with-in and across categories. In the main counterfactual, a ban on high-nicotine e-cigarettes reduces total consumption by 34.8 to 64.2 percent across representative markets and lowers consumer surplus by 44.7 to 70.2 percent. The equilibrium response differs across markets: in some, the ban increases active firms by up to 15.9 percent as reduced big-firm competition creates room for small-firm entry; in others, active firms fall by 12.1 percent. Comparing the endogenous equilibrium with a benchmark that holds firm choices fixed shows that endogenous firm adjustment materially affects entry, product variety, and the magnitude of the consumer-surplus loss. The consumer-surplus cost of the ban establishes a lower bound on the health and externality benefits the policy must deliver to be welfare-improving.

title: Positional Technology: Organizational Hierarchy and Employee Engagement with AI and Automation
affiliations: Columbia Business School and Columbia University - Columbia Business School

detail.title: Positional Technology: Organizational Hierarchy and Employee Engagement with AI and Automation
detail.abstract: We characterize AI and automation as positional technologies whose engagement, support, and associated workplace themes depend not only on occupational tasks, but also on employees' positions within the organizational hierarchy. Using large-scale text data from employee workplace reviews, we document that senior employees reference AI more frequently, describe it with more positive sentiment and promotion focus, and associate it with organizational opportunities. Junior employees reference AI less frequently, describe it with more negative sentiment and prevention focus, and associate it with personal vulnerabilities. Cognitive capacity amplifies these positional differences, while decision-making intensity attenuates them. Outsourcing and traditional automation exhibit similar positional dynamics, although with important differences in the role of cognitive capacity. By examining within-firm heterogeneity across hierarchical levels, our study advances an organizational model of technological engagement that complements existing task-based frameworks and firm-level studies of technology adoption.

detail.abstract: This study examines whether volatility in crude oil prices affects Indonesia’s economy, given the country’s dependence on oil imports. Using Indonesia as the focus of analysis, the paper investigates how significant changes in oil prices over a 15-year period may influence economic and financial indicators. Alongside other econometric variables, the study develops a forecasting model to assess possible future outcomes. Because long-term planning requires more than historical data, the paper also simulates different scenarios to evaluate how changes in key variables may affect Indonesia’s economic outlook. However, forecasting models alone may not fully account for uncertainties that could emerge over the planning horizon. To address this limitation, the study applies a scenario planning framework, enabling policymakers and stakeholders to consider probable and plausible future developments. By combining econometric forecasting with scenario planning, the paper provides insights for Indonesia and other stakeholders to design strategies for managing internal and external economic changes.

publicationDetails.detailsText: Adrian König, From Tariff to Award: Determinants of Court-Awarded Litigation Costs in Swiss Commercial Courts, in: Jusletter as of May 11 2026.

detail.abstract:
This paper provides the first empirical analysis of court-determined litigation costs at Swiss commercial courts. It draws on 976 published judgments from the commercial courts of Zurich and Aargau between 2011 and 2025 and estimates log-linear regression models that link awarded court costs and party compensation to cantonal base tariffs, case characteristics, and procedural complexity indicators. Data extraction for the Zurich subsample relies on an LLM-based pipeline that achieves 99.45% accuracy on a 130-judgment golden set.

The central result is systematic tariff compression. Courts treat the cantonal base tariff as a starting point but do not apply it proportionally: a 10% increase in the base tariff is associated with only approximately 8.9% higher actual court costs and 8.3% higher party compensation. Procedural trajectory dominates deviations on the court cost side. A second exchange of written submissions is associated with roughly 65% higher court costs, settlement hearings with 16% higher costs, and expert reports with 13% higher costs. For party compensation, the cantonal regime explains most variation while procedural indicators contribute little additional power. Approximately 47% of court cost variance and 52% of party compensation variance remain unexplained even in the full specification.

A supplementary ex ante perspective evaluates how precisely litigants can forecast costs at the outset of proceedings. Using only information available at filing, the model achieves a median in-sample forecast error of approximately ±21% for court costs and ±26% for party compensation. The findings have direct implications for litigation cost budgeting, settlement calculus, and the financial provisioning of pending disputes.026

title: Green in the Shadow. The Information View on Green Banking Regulation
affiliations: University of Amsterdam - University of Amsterdam Faculty of Law and University of Wroclaw

detail.title: Green in the Shadow. The Information View on Green Banking Regulation

publicationDetails.journalName: DFG Center for Advanced Studies - Foundations of Law & Finance (LawFin) Working Paper Series

detail.abstract: We investigate the hurdles to the effective implementation of sustainable banking regulation. We argue that existing approaches rest on an implicit assumption of verifiable asset quality, which is inconsistent with the informational structure of banking. Accordingly, we develop an analytical framework centred on structural asset opacity and information asymmetry: banks operate through opaque balance sheets and possess superior information about asset quality relative to both markets and supervisors. This opacity generates moral hazard in the asset classification when regulatory incentives tied to ‘green’ or ‘brown’ labels induce strategic misrepresentation and adverse selection. We recast the main regulatory tools proposed in the literature. The analysis shows that incorporating sustainability objectives into prudential requirements, particularly capital regulation, is prone to distortion under conditions of unverifiable information, while supervisory tools remain constrained by their reliance on  bank-generated data. We advance an alternative approach based on mandatory contractual mechanisms embedded in lending relationships. Properly designed and supervised, these private law tools operate as sorting devices that differentiate between green and brown activities without requiring full information about asset quality.

detail.title: University at Your Doorstep: Local Human Capital Effects of Higher Education Expansion

publicationDetails.detailsText: Ca' Foscari University of Venice, Department of Economics Research Paper Series No. 17/2026

detail.abstract: University systems in many countries expanded by establishing new institutions in areas previously lacking higher education. We study Italy's postwar university expansion, which opened the first faculties in provinces that had never hosted one. Exploiting variation in the timing of these openings across provinces and birth cohorts in an event-study design, we find that local access increased graduation rates by 3.2 percentage points on average across treated cohorts (approximately 26 percent relative to the pre-treatment mean), with a sharp discontinuity of 1.2 percentage points at the enrollment-age threshold. The effect is significant across all urbanization levels and increasing in more urbanized provinces, consistent with complementarities between university access and local labour market conditions. Women benefited disproportionately, though gender gaps in labour market outcomes narrowed by less than those in education. Spillover effects to neighbouring provinces exist but are of secondary magnitude, with the local effect approximately twice the size of the neighbour effect. At the province level, these first openings reduced educational disparities between provinces that gained a university and those that remained unserved.

title: In Search of University Democracy
affiliations: New York University School of Law and Columbia University - Law School

detail.title: In Search of University Democracy

publicationDetails.detailsText: University of Pennsylvania Law Review, Vol. 175, forthcoming

publicationDetails.journalName: Columbia Law School, Public Law & Legal Theory Research Paper Series

detail.abstract:
Virtually all institutions of higher education in the United States share the same basic governance structure. Ultimate authority resides not with faculty, students, staff, or their representatives but with an external board of trustees and the senior management it installs. At private universities, most new trustees are chosen by current trustees. At public universities, most are appointed by politicians. At both, boards are unrepresentative of and unaccountable to the campus community. This governance model does not reliably produce better educational or operational outcomes; it sits in stark tension with universities’ aspirations to be autonomous intellectual communities; and it has been rejected by prominent universities abroad. Why is it ubiquitous here?

This Article identifies and explores the puzzle of the missing alternative: a stakeholder structure that allows core internal constituencies, such as faculty and students, to select a majority of trustees and approve major decisions. Looking backward, the Article considers possible answers to this puzzle—including path dependence, institutional isomorphism, and donor preferences—and argues that they do not fully explain or justify the continued absence of stakeholder universities in the United States. Looking forward, the Article calls attention to the educational, epistemic, economic, and civic benefits that stakeholder governance could bring, along with a number of costs and complications. Finally, the Article outlines different forms that stakeholderism might take and different strategies that reformers might employ. There are no easy or uniform answers to the question of how universities should be run. But at a time when higher education faces mounting threats from political actors at the federal and state levels, there are good reasons to believe that more stakeholder-oriented governance models could help to safeguard the academic mission of universities as well as the democratic capacity of the broader society.

detail.title: A Designed-for-Test Measurement of Discourse-Language Bias in Large Language Model Brand Recommendations

detail.abstract:
This paper reports a designed-for-test measurement of discourse-language bias in large language model (LLM) brand recommendations for premium kitchen knives — a category dominated in production and chef reputation by Japan but mediated in English-language coverage through US/UK food media. Thirty-three brands across four lineages (Japanese, German, American, shared) plus one hybrid (Miyabi) were measured against six pre-registered prompts anchored to Category Entry Points, six frontier models from four labs (Anthropic Claude Sonnet 4.6 and Opus 4.7, OpenAI gpt-5.4-mini and gpt-5.5, Google Gemini 2.5 Flash, xAI Grok 4.1 Fast), and eight runs each (n = 288 successful measurements). Eight hypotheses with explicit numerical thresholds were committed to a pre-registration document locked at git commit d3e0989 prior to any data collection.

The headline lineage-aggregate hypothesis (H1) was disconfirmed at both registry versions. At the locked v1.0 registry (21 brands), Japanese aggregate Presence was 36.2 percent versus German 27.3 percent — an 8.9-point gap in the wrong direction. At the published v1.2 registry (33 brands, 19 Japanese standard plus 1 hybrid, after the registry-revision protocol added boundary-condition makers from the unknown-mentions list), Japanese aggregate fell to 25.7 percent and German held at 27.2 percent — a 1.5-point gap in the predicted direction but below the 5-point partial-confirmation threshold. The lineage-aggregate hypothesis therefore fails consistently across registry construction.

The within-lineage results carry a different signal entirely. Within Japanese, mass-market English-marketed brands (Shun, Global, Mac) surface at 55.2 percent versus 6.8 percent for the fourteen boundary-condition Japanese makers in the canonical scoring — a 48.4-percentage-point gap and approximately 8x ratio. Within German, the boundary case (Güde) appears in zero of 288 measurements while English-marketed German makers (Wüsthof, Henckels) average 62.0 percent. Within the boundary-condition Japanese cohort itself, seven brands clear the 5-percent floor and two stand markedly apart at the upper end: Masamoto at 18.1 percent and Takamura at 16.7 percent — both characterized by substantial US-targeted English-language distribution and chef-endorsed English-media coverage. Of 262 named authority mentions across all 288 measurements, 100 percent are English-language; no Japanese, German, French, or other-language sources surface in any response.

A secondary finding replicates across providers: newer-generation models within both Anthropic (Opus 4.7 versus Sonnet 4.6) and OpenAI (gpt-5.5 versus gpt-5.4-mini) surface boundary-condition Japanese brands at higher rates than their older counterparts — the second cross-category replication of a "newer models surface boundary cases more, not less" pattern in the AIAS measurement program.

The lineage-aggregate failure (H1) and the within-lineage convergence (H3, H5, H8) together motivate a candidate alternative framing: marketing-language coverage as a brand-level mediator of AI brand presence in cross-lingual categories. Brands with substantial English-language marketing infrastructure surface at materially higher rates than equivalently positioned brands without such infrastructure, within every lineage of origin tested. The framing is offered as a candidate hypothesis adjacent to but structurally distinct from existing AI-Surfacing hypotheses (Default Reinforcement; recommendation-slot persistence; freshness-lag). It predicts that brand-level English-marketing investment, not lineage of origin, is the binding variable for AI Presence in cross-lingual categories. Construct validity remains open and is the proposed object of a Phase 3 designed-for-confirmation study.

title: From Self-Deception to Self-Awareness: A Theological and Psychological Framework for Spiritual Formation

detail.title: From Self-Deception to Self-Awareness: A Theological and Psychological Framework for Spiritual Formation
detail.abstract: Self-deception is a pervasive human phenomenon that cuts across philosophy, psychology, sociology, and theology, constituting the deep root of cognitive dysfunction in public life. This article advances three original contributions. First, it integrates Rosenthal's Higher-Order Thought theory (HOT) of consciousness, Kegan's subject-object developmental model, and the biblical narratives of self-deception to construct a three-tier consciousness spectrum-from the child's pure first-order arrest, to the volitional cultivation of not-knowing, to the active suppression of acknowledged truth. Second, taking Paul's call to maturity (1 Cor 13:11; 14:20) as its theological framework, it proposes a developmental moral assessment of self-deception: for adults, selfdeception is a manifestation of sin, and the genuine moral question is whether one is willing to grow up. Third, drawing on Willard's three-tier model of the will as a practical scaffold, it integrates Christian Spiritual Self-Awareness (CSSA) practice with the community's environment of love, proposing an operationalizable pathway from self-deception to self-awareness. The article argues that breaking self-deception is not merely a matter of individual spiritual formation but a concrete way for the church to participate in the renewal of human consciousness and contribute to the common good.

title: Optimal Scheduling of Dengue Vector Control
affiliations: Kansas State University, Kansas State University, Kansas State University and University of Virginia - School of Data Science

detail.title: Optimal Scheduling of Dengue Vector Control
detail.abstract: Dengue transmission is shaped by the population dynamics of the Aedes aegypti mosquito, making vector control a centralstrategy for disease mitigation. The impact of interventions such as larvicide, adulticide, and breeding-site reduction depends critically ontheir timing under fluctuating environmental conditions. We build on a high-fidelity, non-Markovian mechanistic model of the Aedes lifecycle that captures stage-structured, temperature-dependent developmental delays, and mortality, and extend it to incorporate multiplevector control measures. Rather than using continuous abstract control amplitudes as in standard optimal control formulations, weintroduce intervention-specific temporal profiles that better reflect operational practice. We then develop an adjoint-based gradientdescent framework to compute the optimal timing of a sequence of interventions by minimizing the time-dependent dengue reproductionnumber, R0. Numerical simulations based on seasonal temperature data from Miami, Florida, show that appropriately timed combinationsof interventions can substantially suppress transmission risk, with outcomes strongly influenced by seasonal temperature variation andintervention duration. We further propose embedding the resulting optimization framework within a Model Predictive Control architecture,yielding a closed-loop approach for real-time, surveillance-driven vector management under environmental and operational uncertainty.

title: Comparing Spatial Modeling Methods for Surface Prediction

detail.title: Comparing Spatial Modeling Methods for Surface Prediction
detail.abstract: Predicting surfaces is a crucial aspect in infrastructure projects, particularly in road construction. Currently, technological advancements allow for the creation of new automated algorithms that improve accuracy. This study intends to use spatial modeling methods to predict surfaces, this can be achieved by determining which of the interpolators is best appropriate for surface prediction. The used methodology includes data collection using real and statistical surfaces, surface modeling, as well as statistical analysis. Results reveal that the used surfaces are best modeled using Ordinary Kriging and Splines models. Using the findings of this study, surveyors and civil engineers can enhance the accuracy of earthwork volume calculation. Moreover, results could be utilized to benefit other fields such as environmental and hydrological studies.

detail.title: Hedge Ratio Estimation and Risk-Return Dissociation in Pairs Trading: Kalman Filtering under Structural Instability

detail.abstract: When two equities share a long-run co-movement relationship, the ratio of their price sensitivities (the hedge ratio) determines the directional exposure of a pairs trading position. In practice hedge ratios drift as macroeconomic regimes shift, rendering static estimates stale. This paper characterises how the mode of hedge ratio estimation shapes the risk-return profile of pairs trading strategies, rather than asking whether pairs trading is profitable in aggregate. Two hypotheses are tested with econometric discipline: does Kalman-filtered dynamic estimation statistically reduce tail-risk relative to static OLS (H1), and does a two-state Hidden Markov Model (HMM) regime filter further reduce drawdown (H2)? We evaluate seven estimation branches on 50 S&P 500 equities across the structurally demanding 2020-2024 window, which compresses four macroeconomic regimes (COVID-19 shock, quantitative easing recovery, Federal Reserve rate-hike cycle, and AI-driven sector concentration) into five calendar years. This window is an intentionally selected high-instability evaluation period; results should be interpreted as conditional on this environment and may not generalise to calmer or longer samples. A walk-forward cross-validation design with 14 rolling out-of-sample folds prevents in-sample overfitting; BCa bootstrap confidence intervals on the annualised Sharpe ratio and Wilcoxon signed-rank tests on fold-level differences provide formal inference. In this demanding environment, all seven branches produce negative net-of-cost fold-mean Sharpe ratios, confirming that 28-bps round-trip transaction costs consume gross alpha at the 2.3-day average holding periods generated by the Kalman branches. Static OLS achieves a foldmean Sharpe of-0.157 versus-2.080 for Kalman (OLS dominant in 12 of 14 folds), driven 1 by the Kalman filter's 54% higher trade turnover (932 vs. 607 pooled trades) that amplifies cost drag. Despite lower net Sharpe, Kalman reduces fold-mean maximum drawdown by 71% relative to OLS (-0.31% vs.-1.07%), a dissociation of return from risk that is the paper's central empirical finding. For H2, HMM conditioning further reduces fold-mean MaxDD by 30% (to-0.22%, Wilcoxon p < 0.001) while cutting trade frequency by 45%. A mechanism decomposition (Branch D) shows Kalman's drawdown advantage is consistent with a structural explanation: short holding periods alone do not replicate it; a posterior variance entry gate (Branch F) partially repairs signal quality (52.7%→54.8% win rate) and improves fold-mean Sharpe to-1.38. The estimated Kalman-OLS cost breakeven is 6-7 bps one-way, suggesting that Kalman may be competitive at direct-market-access execution costs while retaining its drawdown advantage.

detail.abstract:
This working paper examines implementation disparities within the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline system and argues that the primary limitations of 988 stem not from the concept itself, but from fragmented state-level infrastructure, uneven operational capacity, and inconsistent implementation systems.

While 988 established a nationally standardized front-end access point for mental health crisis response, backend crisis infrastructure, including mobile crisis teams, stabilization centers, workforce capacity, and interstate coordination, remains highly variable across states. As a result, individuals who access the same national hotline may experience substantially different levels of care depending on their geographic location.

Drawing upon implementation theory, public administration frameworks, and policyscape analysis, this paper proposes a federal-state partnership model for incentives designed to strengthen crisis response infrastructure while preserving state-level flexibility. The paper argues that achieving equitable crisis care requires moving beyond symbolic policy adoption toward sustained institutional investment, implementation support, and coordinated infrastructure development.

title: Estimating and Assessing Identification of Structural Models via Deep Learning
affiliations: University of Southern California - Marshall School of Business and University of Pennsylvania - The Wharton School

detail.title: Estimating and Assessing Identification of Structural Models via Deep Learning
detail.abstract: We study using neural nets to process an entire dataset and produce an estimate for a structural econometric model (e.g., discrete choice, consumer search). To make training feasible, the neural net uses an architecture that exploits the i.i.d. structure common in empirical data. We show that with sufficient training on simulated datasets, this neural net converges to the full-information posterior. The approach allows accurate, full-information estimation for models where likelihood simulation is impractical or challenging. It also provides a tool to assess empirical identification. We apply it to a sequential search model with unobserved heterogeneity.

title: When AI Is Not Force Majeure -The Hangzhou Ruling (Zhou v. Tech Co., 2026) and the Legal Limits of Causal Imputation of Automation in Labor Law

detail.title: When AI Is Not Force Majeure -The Hangzhou Ruling (Zhou v. Tech Co., 2026) and the Legal Limits of Causal Imputation of Automation in Labor Law
detail.abstract: This paper analyzes the ruling of the Hangzhou Intermediate People's Court of 28 April 2026 (Zhou v. Tech Co.), which declared unlawful the dismissal of a worker whose position had been absorbed by an AI system based on large language models. It is argued that the ruling's conceptual contribution lies less in concrete labor protection than in the underlying interpretive operation: the refusal to treat AI adoption as a "major change in objective circumstances" equivalent to force majeure. That refusal preserves a classical principle of imputationtechnological decisions remain business decisionsand forecloses a possible doctrine of exculpatory technological fatalism. Parallels are drawn with Argentine labor law (art. 247 LCT) and with the EU regime (AI Act 2024/1689 and Platform Work Directive 2024/2831), and the case is read as comparative confirmation of the principle of inverse externality: technological risk is business risk.

title: Old Space, New Space: A Commercial Revolution in Innovation?
affiliations: University of Toronto - Rotman School of Management and University of Calgary

detail.title: Old Space, New Space: A Commercial Revolution in Innovation?
detail.abstract:
The emergence of firms like SpaceX and Blue Origin has made space a leading example of how private enterprise drives innovation, marking what many see as a sharp break between Old Space and New Space. Yet little systematic evidence documents when the transition to this new phase of space innovation occurred and which firms drove it. We use patent data to provide this measurement and find that the largest surge in space innovation occurred in the 1990s, coinciding with demand-side market creation, and preceding the entry of high-profile startups after 2005. Throughout this period and since, incumbent aerospace firms account for most of the space-related patenting, with entrants contributing a growing but minority share. The same geographic regions that dominated space innovation during the post-Apollo era remain dominant today. These patterns are consistent with directed technical change: incumbents direct R&D toward policy-created markets accessible from existing capabilities, while entrants bring science-based insights into domains requiring new paradigms. Our findings suggest that New Space is more closely connected to Old Space than prevailing narratives imply, and that government's most consequential role in space innovation may lie in constructing appropriable markets. We make patent data on space-related technologies available for future research.

title: Sophisticated Borrowing Constraints and Macroeconomic Dynamics
affiliations: New York University (NYU) - New York University, University of California, Berkeley, University of Chicago - Booth School of Business,  and New York University (NYU) - Department of Economics

detail.title: Sophisticated Borrowing Constraints and Macroeconomic Dynamics
detail.abstract:
In traditional macro-finance models, firms' debt contracts impose hard borrowing constraints, which require indiscriminate reductions of borrowing and investment when adverse shocks tighten these limits, giving rise to financial acceleration. We study the macroeconomic implications of "sophisticated borrowing constraints" akin to financial covenants among large U.S. nonfinancial firms, commonly specified based on firms' debt relative to operating earnings. We model these constraints as debt thresholds that trigger a transfer of control rights to creditors when they are violated, in which case creditors influence firms' decisions to maximize their value instead of cutting credit unconditionally to adhere to fixed ratios. At the micro level, our model is quantitatively consistent with empirical patterns of investment and earnings around covenant violations. At the macro level, sophisticated borrowing constraints do not generate financial acceleration, because constraint tightening and violations do not induce creditors to downscale firms indiscriminately.

title: The Psychology of Macroeconomic Expectations
affiliations: University of Oxford - Said Business School, , SKEMA Business School, Harvard University, Harvard University - Department of Economics and De Nederlandsche Bank

detail.title: The Psychology of Macroeconomic Expectations
detail.abstract:
We present a model of “animal spirits” in which context and emotions affect macroeconomic beliefs by shaping which experiences people recall to simulate similar future aggregate states. We test this mechanism by priming Dutch National Bank Survey respondents to recall personal financial or health adversities before eliciting inflation and home price expectations. The treatment causes instability in beliefs and reasoning tied to the measured similarity of the primed experiences to different macro states. This similarity structure also accounts for heterogeneity in beliefs and reasoning based on a range of other personal experiences we measure. The model micro founds several features of macroeconomic beliefs, including narratives, and yields a “confidence multiplier”: spending by some agents cues optimistic context for others, raising their spending.

title: Divergence in Climate Change Communication: LLM-Based Evidence from the IPCC and the Press
affiliations: Department of Economics,  and University of San Andres (UdeSA)

detail.title: Divergence in Climate Change Communication: LLM-Based Evidence from the IPCC and the Press
detail.abstract:
Public summaries of IPCC climate assessments lean toward the more severe end of the technical evidence. The pattern appears at two stages: the IPCC’s lead authors and member governments produce the Summary for Policymakers (SPM) from the Technical Summary (TS), and newspapers then cover the SPM. We use LLMs to score about 114,000 matched claim pairs from all six Assessment Reports (1990 to 2023) and ten major US and UK outlets. Both stages systematically shift toward the more severe end of the source while staying inside the IPCC’s accepted scientific ranges. The shift comes mainly from emphasizing higher-impact magnitudes within reported ranges, less from uncertainty compression, and almost none from selecting worst-case emissions scenarios. Left- and right-leaning outlets show similar patterns.

detail.abstract:
Monitoring systems for disaster prevention are costly, and measuring benefits is difficult when monitoring effort is endogenous. We provide the first causal estimate of one such system's impact using three decades of desert locust monitoring data. We document conflict-induced interruptions to monitoring in remote breeding areas, reconstruct how infestations spread to populated areas, and show that exposure to locust swarms around birth decreases child height-for-age, increasing stunting risk by over 7 percentage points. Political inclusion is widely believed to improve governance, motivating the creation of elected representatives for highly localized constituencies. We provide new county-level estimates of intergenerational mobility, covering multiple economic concepts: total income, labor income, homeownership, housing wealth, and total wealth. This is possible via small-area estimation techniques and linked survey and administrative data covering millions of U.S. children born between 1978 and 1986. title: Proposed Mergers Where Efficiencies Are Needed Most Might Be the Least Likely to Deliver Them
affiliations: Columbia University, International Monetary Fund (IMF) and University of Chicago - Booth School of Business

detail.title: Proposed Mergers Where Efficiencies Are Needed Most Might Be the Least Likely to Deliver Them
detail.abstract:
Mergers are commonly evaluated by weighing their expected market power effects against any efficiency gains they create. The larger the market power effect of a proposed merger, the larger must be any efficiencies for it to raise social welfare. We show selection into merger proposal distorts the observed relationship between market power and efficiency effects. Even if market power and efficiency gains are independent (or even positively correlated) across all potential mergers, they will generally be negatively related among proposed mergers. This is because parties propose to merge only if the merger’s expected profitability exceeds a threshold, so the underlying components of profitability become substitutes in clearing that hurdle. It does not rely on managerial bias, behavioral frictions, or strategic misrepresentation. We demonstrate this negative correlation is present under very general conditions when the two effects are uncorrelated among all mergers. We also characterize conditions where this still holds even in the presence of positive underlying correlations and firms’ uncertainty about their own merger’s profitability. Policies that might raise the selection hurdle for proposed mergers do not alleviate the negative correlation; indeed, they would exacerbate it. Our analysis has direct implications for interpreting empirical merger retrospectives and for evaluating efficiency defenses in antitrust policy.

detail.abstract:
This paper introduces the Aggregate Perceived Risk (APR) framework, a unified valuation architecture that mathematically links classical rational expectations with behavioral finance. The core innovation is a shift from the traditional linear, additive pricing model, where price equals intrinsic value plus or minus extrinsic adjustments, to a geometric, exponential formulation in which perception scales value rather than adjusting it. By placing Aggregate Perceived Risk in the denominator and raising it to a structural exponent, the model produces a measurable Perception Gap that captures the nonlinear influence of collective comfort, liquidity, friction, and capital concentration. This structure explains why markets routinely exhibit bubbles, crashes, fat tails, and violent regime shifts that linear models cannot mathematically reproduce and therefore misclassify as anomalies.

By incorporating perception and structural constraints directly into the pricing mechanism, the APR framework provides a probabilistic observational method that allows practitioners to gauge when the perception gap is widening to a degree that makes a directional reversion toward intrinsic value increasingly likely. Because the Perception Gap expands and contracts in systematic, quantifiable ways, the model establishes conditions under which persistent alpha becomes attainable through the detection of perception‑driven mispricing. APR therefore transforms financial analysis from a qualitative description of sentiment into a rigorous, structurally grounded science of market dynamics.

title: Keju, Not Violence: How the Medieval Chinese Aristocracy Declined in the Tang Dynasty Long Before the Huang Chao Rebellion
affiliations: New York University (NYU) - Wilf Family Department of Politics

contentType.other: Translation of a published article in a top Chinese journal

detail.abstract:
When and how did the medieval Chinese aristocracy decline? Generations of historians have argued that the political power of the aristocracy was gradually displaced by the imperial examination system (Keju) during the Tang dynasty. In recent decades, however, other historians have alleged that aristocratic political dominance persisted until the Huang Chao Rebellion at the end of the Tang, pointing to the ostensibly stable share of aristocrats among high ranking officials across the dynasty. This article identifies several fundamental flaws in the statistical reasoning underlying claims of aristocratic persistence, including conceptual ambiguity, definitional tautology, misinterpretation of conditional probabilities, and the absence of control variables in existing quantitative analyses. Using multivariate statistical models applied to a large sample of Tang tomb epitaphs, drawn from essentially the same epitaph based evidence used in prior quantitative studies but analyzed with more adequate methods, I show that the political advantage associated with aristocratic pedigree declined rapidly after the early Tang, while the net premium associated with Keju credentials increased steadily over time, even after controlling for aristocratic influence. Both trends-the erosion of pedigree-based advantage and the rising importance of Keju-were already underway more than two centuries before the Huang Chao Rebellion and other violent upheavals marking the end of the Tang and its immediate successor polities. These new findings leave the social and political dimensions of the Tang-Song Transition thesis on shaky ground.

This article is an English translation of a study previously published in Historical Research (历史研究), with minor adaptations for an English-language audience.

detail.abstract: The Bureau of Labor Statistics U-3 unemployment rate captures a single dimension of labor market health. This paper constructs a County-Level Comprehensive Labor Underutilization Index (CLUI) using Fay-Herriot small-area estimation on 3,082 U.S. counties. The index combines three layers of distress: official unemployment, labor force non-participation, and poverty-wage employment. Nationally, poverty-wage employment accounts for 37 percent of the CLUI, the participation gap for 25 percent, and unemployment for just 15 percent. The Fay-Herriot EBLUP achieves 78 percent variance reduction over direct survey estimates. Five contributions follow. First, the CLUI predicts county premature mortality 3.6 times better than U-3 (R-squared = 0.417 versus 0.116) and disability non-participation 3.1 times better (Rsquared = 0.419 versus 0.134); neither outcome enters the CLUI construction. Under spatial buffered cross-validation, the CLUI reduces premature death prediction error by 39.3 percent. Second, Vuong (1989) and Williams (1959) tests confirm CLUI superiority in 12 of 20 pairwise comparisons against five competing indices. Third, spatial autocorrelation is substantial (Moran's I = 0.603); a spatial Fay-Herriot extension preserves baseline rankings (Spearman rho = 0.987), and the Chen (2026) diagnostic indicates that standard shrinkage understates distress in small rural counties. Fourth, 292 hidden-distress counties representing 6.6 million residents have official unemployment below 4 percent but severe comprehensive underutilization. Fifth, these counties shifted toward the Republican ticket in 2024, though this association does not survive spatial HAC correction. Results are stable across ten robustness checks.

detail.abstract: Forced migration and statelessness constitute significant yet often underexamined structural drivers of conflict affecting peace and security across Africa. While frequently framed as humanitarian challenges, both phenomena generate profound governance, legal, and socioeconomic implications capable of intensifying instability where institutional protection mechanisms remain weak. This essay clarifies core concepts relating to forced migration, internal displacement, refugee protection, and statelessness, and evaluates the effectiveness of international, regional, and subregional legal frameworks, including the 1951 Refugee Convention, the 1954 and 1961 Statelessness Conventions, the 1969 Organization of African Unity (OAU) Refugee Convention, and the 2009 Kampala Convention on internally displaced persons. Through doctrinal legal analysis and comparative case studies drawn from the Lake Chad Basin, Côte d'Ivoire, and the Sudan-South Sudan context, the study demonstrates how exclusion from nationality, weak civil registration systems, and inconsistent policy implementation contribute to grievances capable of reinforcing conflict dynamics. Evidence suggests that large-scale displacement may initially intensify competition over resources and heighten communal tensions, particularly where legal identity systems and socioeconomic inclusion mechanisms are insufficiently developed. However, inclusive legal frameworks and coordinated governance approaches may generate stabilizing effects, including economic participation and strengthened social cohesion. The essay identifies key policy gaps including securitization of migration, political resistance to nationality reform, and limited institutional coordination among regional actors. It concludes that strengthening nationality protection, civil registration systems, and regional legal harmonization constitutes an important preventive peacebuilding strategy capable of reducing structural vulnerabilities associated with forced migration and statelessness in Africa.

detail.abstract:
Opaque assets in mergers and acquisitions (M&A) create the need for unique transaction structures such as contingent value rights (CVRs) and earnouts. Prior research exposes two main functions of these contingent contracts. The first is to align post acquisitions incentives and retain human capital. The second is to bridge valuation disagreements, allowing inher- ently riskier assets to sell by spreading uncertainty across parties. The capital-intensive and risk-centric biopharmaceutical industry makes it an ideal setting to explore these functions. This paper aims to address the gap in M&A contracting literature by examining CVRs in biopharmaceutical acquisitions to analyze how contingent payment structures influence drug approval.

This paper compiles 313 biopharma transactions from Evaluate Pharma’s transaction database and assesses their post-acquisition success measure through primary asset approval. The data is comprised of 91 transactions structured with a CVR and 222 with upfront payment. It then models out a linear probability model (LPM), logit, and propensity score model (PSM) to compare the percentage of approved deals. The regression models control for three main determinants of drug approval as found in the literature: inherent drug risk, resource risk, and timing risk. These models produce 13% to 19% lower drug approval in CVR transactions, indicating that contingent contracting in biopharma is primarily used to bridge valuation disagreements and thus is more densely used in transactions with greater underlying risk. While this does not refute the possibility of an incentive aligning hypothesis, the findings provide empirical support that CVRs in biopharma transactions serve to bridge valuation and spread risk for assets with extreme uncertainty.
