detail.title: The Agentic Law Firm: Competence, Supervision, Confidentiality, and Conflicts Across Six Levels of AI Autonomy
detail.abstract:
In March 2026, an Orange County Superior Court sanctioned an attorney whose AI system autonomously generated and filed a motion containing fabricated citations without the attorney’s review. The AI did not hallucinate a single case in a research query. It drafted a pleading, selected authorities, assembled arguments, signed the attorney’s name to the filing, and submitted it to the court. The attorney learned of the fabrications when opposing counsel raised them. This is not a hallucination problem. It is a supervision problem. And it is not a problem the Model Rules of Professional Conduct were designed to address.

Existing scholarship on artificial intelligence (AI) in legal practice treats AI tools as nonlawyers under Model Rule 5.3, supervised under the same framework applied to paralegals, contract attorneys, and other human assistants. American Bar Association (ABA) Formal Opinion 512 adopts this uniform treatment. That framework absorbed the typewriter, word processing, electronic research, and even retrieval-augmented generative AI. But agentic AI systematically inverts four assumptions embedded in the supervision doctrine: that nonlawyer assistance operates at human speed under continuous attorney direction, within observable scope, with ex-ante conflict identification. When those assumptions fail, the doctrine’s gap-filling mechanisms fail with them.

This Article proposes a framework that calibrates Model Rules compliance to AI autonomy level through two analytical axes. First, a six-level autonomy spectrum (Level 0 through Level 5) adapted from the Society of Automotive Engineers J3016 taxonomy and the emerging AI governance consensus of DeepMind’s Levels of AGI and the Cloud Security Alliance’s Agentic Trust Framework, calibrated to the doctrinal task of Model Rules compliance. Second, a dual-vector framework that distinguishes substantive legal practice (Vector A: competence, communication, candor, conflicts) from firm operations (Vector B: confidentiality infrastructure, trust accounting, marketing). The two vectors carry different ceilings: Vector A permits autonomy through Level 2 with limited Level 3 deployment for non-judgment components; Vector B permits autonomy through Level 4 under bounded-autopilot architecture.

The framework produces five categorical bright lines the Rules assign to named attorneys by text and that no level of AI autonomy can cross: rendering legal advice under Rule 2.1; Rule 11 and Rule 26(g) certification; privilege calls under Rule 1.6; substantive communication judgment under Rule 1.4(b); and Rule 1.7 and 1.9 conflict clearance. The Article identifies a substance-touch rule for mixed-vector communications: any communication that transmits, summarizes, or characterizes substantive legal analysis is Vector A regardless of the channel through which it is delivered. The Article identifies a combinatorial compounding problem that produces the Level 5 categorical impossibility for substantive practice and that limits Level 4 deployment to operationally bounded tasks. The Article identifies six architectural boundaries that define bounded autopilot operation.

The prediction is eighteen months: at least one state bar will adopt autonomy-level calibration in a formal opinion, and at least one reported sanctions decision will cite the bright-line framework. If either condition fails to occur within the window, the framework is falsified.

detail.title: Dynamic Influencer Identity
detail.abstract: Consumers form impressions of influencers not from a single message, but from sequences of signals encountered over time.  How does the variation across this history shape consumer response?  A multimethod investigation, combining text embeddings on nearly 20,000 sponsored posts from 940 influencers with preregistered controlled experiments, reveals an inverted Ushaped relationship between identity breadth and engagement: moderate breadth outperforms both narrow and highly diffuse identities.  Taking a dynamic view, new content performs best when it deviates moderately from prior posts, with shifts into related product categories outperforming both repetition and moves across distant categories.  Moderate variation works because it balances coherence with new information, sustaining interest while preserving perceived authenticity.  Further, the effects depend on influencer lifecycle and post goals.  Together, these findings reconceptualize identity as a dynamic, cumulative inference and demonstrate how automated text analysis can be used to study identity dynamics.

detail.abstract: This paper introduces the Deal Dashboard™, a structured pre-commitment instrument designed to help deal teams, boards, and their advisors assess offers systematically before accepting them. Drawing on research in behavioral decision science, organizational behavior, aviation safety, surgical medicine, professional baseball, emergency medicine, intelligence analysis, and corporate law, it argues that contemporary dealmaking suffers from precisely the same gap between prevailing practice and demonstrable best practice that once afflicted commercial aviation, surgery, and professional baseball-and that structured instruments can close that gap with comparable results. A central organizing concept introduced here is the framework pivot: the phenomenon, observed across multiple high-stakes fields, in which a domain reaches an inflection point where the adoption of structured best-practice instruments produces dramatic, measurable improvements in outcomes-not by replacing expertise, experience, or intuition, but by ensuring they are applied systematically at critical decision moments. Aviation, surgery, baseball, emergency medicine, intelligence analysis, and nursing have each undergone a framework pivot. Dealmaking has not. This paper argues that it is overdue, and that the instruments to enable it already exist. The paper proceeds in four parts. Part I documents the scale of deal failure across M&A, joint ventures, infrastructure projects, ERP implementations, and digital transformations, and identifies the cognitive and structural causes. A steelman analysis of optimistic M&A research is presented, and both the optimistic and pessimistic cases are shown to point toward the same conclusion: systematic process discipline, not expertise alone, is the operative variable distinguishing successful from unsuccessful deal outcomes. Part II reviews how framework pivots have transformed performance in other high-stakes fields, with particular attention to the role of Crew Resource Management in aviation, the surgical safety checklist, analytics-based decision-making in professional baseball, Advanced Trauma Life Support in emergency medicine, Structured Analytic Techniques in intelligence analysis, and early warning scoring systems in nursing. Part III presents the Deal Dashboard™ overview, field evidence, and case reconstructions. Part IV analyzes the fiduciary and legal dimensions of deal failure. Part V describes the Deal Dashboard™ architecture, explaining how each design feature addresses a specific cognitive, structural, or legal vulnerability identified in the preceding analysis.

title: Quantifying Spirituality as a Moderator of Food Security in Climate-Vulnerable Communities in the Gulf of Guinea

detail.title: Quantifying Spirituality as a Moderator of Food Security in Climate-Vulnerable Communities in the Gulf of Guinea
detail.abstract: Dominant frameworks for understanding climate adaptation in the Global South have long privileged material, infrastructural, and institutional variables, systematically neglecting the socially embedded systems of meaning through which vulnerable communities actually navigate ecological uncertainty. Spirituality, despite its deep embeddedness within the communal fabric of West and Central African life, has remained at the analytical margins of climate-food security scholarship, acknowledged descriptively, operationalized rarely. Drawing on the Afrobarometer Round 9 Survey (2021-2023; N = 11,847) merged with Notre Dame Global Adaptation Initiative vulnerability scores across nine Gulf of Guinea nations, this study quantifies spirituality as a moderating variable in the relationship between climate vulnerability and household food insecurity. Hierarchical moderated regression analysis confirms that climate vulnerability exerts a large positive effect on food insecurity (β = .31, p < .001), and that spirituality significantly attenuates this relationship (β =-.09, p < .001). Crucially, communal spiritual embeddedness, operationalized as institutional trust in religious leaders, produces a moderating effect more than twice as powerful as individual devotional practice (β =-.14 versus β =-.06), with the difference statistically significant on bootstrap comparison. These findings reposition communally organized spirituality as a measurable component of adaptive capacity, advancing an empirically grounded argument that climate resilience in the Gulf of Guinea is as much a function of social meaning as it is of material resource.

detail.abstract:
Background: Low-dose computed tomography (LDCT) reduces lung cancer mortality, but real-world uptake remains low. This study evaluated a village doctor-led LDCT screening program in rural China to identify implementation determinants and stakeholder preferences for future scale-up.

Methods: An exploratory sequential mixed-methods study was conducted. Semi-structured interviews with healthcare providers and older adults were analyzed using thematic analysis and mapped to the Consolidated Framework for Implementation Research. Best–Worst Scaling surveys assessed stakeholder preferences. Qualitative and quantitative findings were integrated to identify optimization strategies.

Findings: A total of 42 participants completed interviews and 506 completed surveys. Facilitators included integration into routine practice, village doctor leadership, government and collective-economy subsidies, and flexible LDCT options. Barriers included increased workload, limited screening awareness, existing medical expenses, insufficient promotion, and low trust in township hospitals. Healthcare providers prioritized limited screening awareness (β=2.32, 95% CI: 2.20, 2.44) and low trust in township hospitals (β=1.97, 95% CI: 1.85, 2.09), while older adults prioritized collective-economy subsidies (β=4.73, 95% CI: 4.22, 5.24) and flexible LDCT options (β=4.22, 95% CI: 3.73, 4.71). Four optimization areas were identified: workflow improvement, strengthened financial support, tailored communication and service options, and individualized education and trust-building.

Interpretation: Optimizing LDCT upgrading in rural primary healthcare requires alignment with both stakeholder preferences and local implementation context. Future scale-up should prioritize individualized education, sustainable financial support, workflow optimization, and village doctor-led model strategies.

title: Neurocognitive and Evolutionary Architecture of Visual Perceptual Completion: Mechanisms of Sensory Interpolation and Object Synthesis

detail.title: Neurocognitive and Evolutionary Architecture of Visual Perceptual Completion: Mechanisms of Sensory Interpolation and Object Synthesis

detail.abstract: The human visual system constantly encounters fragmented sensory inputs due to environmental occlusions and anatomical deficits like the blind spot. Despite this, perception remains phenomenologically continuous. This paper comprehensively reviews the neurocognitive, developmental, and evolutionary architectures underlying visual perceptual completion-the brain's capacity to synthesize complete object representations from partial ("half-seen") stimuli. We trace the historical foundations of Gestalt psychology to modern neurophysiological discoveries, distinguishing between modal and amodal completion mechanisms. 1 Evidence demonstrates that while early visual cortices (V1/V2) utilize structurally driven isomorphic interpolation, the lateral occipital complex (LOC) and inferotemporal (IT) cortex govern knowledge-driven, symbolic completion. 2 Furthermore, this review examines the extreme manifestation of top-down priors through "one-shot perceptual learning," detailing recent ultra-high-field fMRI and intracranial EEG findings that localize these instantaneous priors to the high-level visual cortex. Framed within the Bayesian predictive coding hypothesis and evolutionary error management theory, we argue that visual completion is not merely a neural error, but a critical, metabolically expensive adaptation driven by the ecological arms race of predator-prey dynamics and camouflage.

detail.abstract: Mobile users are increasingly engaging with edutainment gaming apps in formal and informal contexts. They are drawn to them for their educational and entertainment aspects. In this light, this study validates the Theory of Planned Behavior's key measures and integrates them with game narratives and game aesthetics constructs to better understand the extent to which psychological and gaming design factors are predicting the individuals' intentions to play with these learning technologies. The data were gathered through a survey questionnaire from one hundred eighty-six (n = 186) respondents, who were higher education students in a Southern European university. The quantitative findings analyzed through partial least squares (PLS) revealed that the gamers appreciate the edutainment platforms' audiovisual effects as well as their storylines and narratives. The results reported that mobile users enjoyed playing with entertaining learning apps. Respondents indicated that they were willing to continue their gameplay in the future. In conclusion, this contribution raises awareness on the important synergies between gaming design elements and behavioral dimensions driving the users' engagement with edutainment apps. It puts forward a robust theoretical framework that is empirically-grounded.

title: Drawn In, Pushed Back: Dual-Route Consumer Responses to AI Virtual Streamers in Live-Streaming E-Commerce

detail.title: Drawn In, Pushed Back: Dual-Route Consumer Responses to AI Virtual Streamers in Live-Streaming E-Commerce
detail.abstract: In live-streaming e-commerce (LSC), the same AI virtual streamers (AVS) can make consumers feel attended to and willing to buy, while they may also evoke feelings of being monitored, treated unfairly, or subjected to excessive persuasion. This research explains this tension by developing a dual-route account of consumer response to AVS. We argue that perceived responsiveness is linked to a relational–approach route in which consumers infer social presence, empathy, and warmth, which in turn is associated with higher purchase intention. Meanwhile, perceived injustice is linked to a defensive–avoidance route in which consumers infer intrusiveness risk and privacy disclosure risk, which in turn is associated with higher resistance intention. We further theorize algorithm aversion as a proposed interpretive gate that shapes how consumers decode AVS cues: higher aversion is associated with a weaker tendency to read responsiveness as relational warmth and a stronger tendency to read injustice as defensive risk. Across two studies, a 2 × 2 online scenario experiment and a survey-based model test, we find that both response routes operate as theorized and that the findings are consistent with the proposed dual-route account. The commercial decisions of consumers depend on how they interpret the approach and avoidance meanings embedded in LSC.

title: Digital Public Infrastructure and the Political Economy of Artificial Intelligence: Public Capability and Contestable Governance

detail.title: Digital Public Infrastructure and the Political Economy of Artificial Intelligence: Public Capability and Contestable Governance
detail.abstract:
Digital Public Infrastructure (DPI) is often presented as a technical foundation for digital government: identity systems, payment rails, registries, data exchanges, and service platforms that enable public and private services at scale. This chapter advances a critical political economy account of DPI, arguing that it is better understood as a durable public capability through which states organise recognition, entitlement, value transfer, information exchange, and administrative coordination. Its public character is not guaranteed by openness, scale, or state sponsorship; it is produced through governance, legal authority, standards, procurement, accountability, and democratic contestability.

The integration of artificial intelligence intensifies these stakes. AI turns DPI from infrastructure that records, authenticates, and connects into infrastructure that classifies, predicts, prioritises, recommends, and judges. The chapter conceptualises this shift as the emergence of public inference infrastructure and the concerns that AI-enabled DPI redistributes power among states, firms, and citizens through control over data, compute, models, standards, and assurance. It also analyses tensions between efficiency and due process, sovereignty and dependency, innovation and enclosure, and automation and accountability. The chapter concludes that AI-enabled DPI must be governed as public power: auditable, rights-preserving, resilient, and open to meaningful redress. Only then can it serve legitimate democratic and developmental ends.

detail.abstract: Current models of human functioning typically distribute regulation across partially independent cognitive, emotional, biological, behavioral and environmental subsystems. Although systems theory, predictive processing, cybernetics, and computational psychiatry have relatively advanced understanding of adaptive regulation, no unified framework currently formalizes identity stability as the primary generative and regulatory variable governing multi-domain human function coherence This paper introduces the Human Integrated Living Dynamics Theory (HILDT), an axiomatic multi-domain framework proposing Identity Stability (I) as the primitive coherence field underlying human functioning system dynamics. Within HILDT, cognition, emotion, behavior, biology and environmental adaptation, are conceptualized as dependent projections of a unified identity stability coherence structure rather than independent causal subsystems. The theory introduces two derived dimensions: Identity Stability Depth (ISD), representing internal coherence integrity across dynamic self-states, and Identity Stability Length (ISL), representing continuity of coherence across changing external environments and relational systems. An axiomatic mathematical formulation is used in which multi-domain Identity Stability is governed by variance-constrained identity stability coherence dynamics. The framework proposes that adaptive functioning emerges through maintenance of a bounded cross-domain variance, while dysfunction arises from coherence fragmentation, desynchronization, or instability propagation across projected domains. HILDT provides a unified Identity Stability-centered architecture for modeling human adaptive dynamics and offers a potential foundation for future empirical operationalization, computational simulation, and multi-domain systems research.

detail.title: Smart Integrated Drainage Monitoring System for Urban Resilience: An IoT-Based Innovation for Zimbabwean Cities
detail.abstract: The rapid urbanization coupled with the aging infrastructure and lack of resources makes drainage management of urban centres in Africa a critical issue. This paper provides the design, implementation, and high-quality assessment of a Smart Integrated Drainage and Sewage Monitoring and Control System (SIDSMCS) customized to the Zimbabwean urban environments. Based on Design Science Research approach, a low-cost IoT solution was built, which combines ESP32 microcontrollers, hybrid communication (Wi-Fi/LoRa/GSM), solar power resiliency, and predictive analytics. The prototype was implemented in 3 high-density locations in Harare in 2023-2024 rainy season. Findings show that there were substantial improvements: response time dropped by 5.2 to 1.5 days (71 percent improvement), 70 percent of possible overflows avoided, 85percent prediction accuracy of blockages, and 73 percent reduction in cost per intervention. Technical evaluation was done thoroughly, consisting of sensor calibration statistics, uncertainty quantification, fault tolerance mechanisms, and economic sensitivity analysis. The proposed system incorporates predictive algorithms and delivers results that match, and in certain respects may surpass, those of smart drainage solutions deployed globally, while operating with drastically reduced resource requirements. This provides empirical evidence that supports the viability of context-specific smart infrastructure in African urban centres.

detail.abstract:
Purpose: This paper presents a deep-case analysis of Saudi Arabia’s Infrastructure-First AI Governance Model - the first of three GCC governance archetypes identified in Pillai (2026c). It examines the structural logic, empirical evidence, strategic strengths, and governance vulnerabilities of building AI sovereignty through infrastructure investment ahead of regulatory framework development, using the HUMAIN programme as the primary case study.
Saudi Arabia is executing the most capital-intensive sovereign AI programme in the developing world. Within twelve months spanning May 2025 to May 2026, the Kingdom launched HUMAIN - a $100 billion PIF-owned AI company - produced ALLaM 34B (independently verified as the most advanced Arabic large language model built in the Arab world), broke ground on the world’s largest government data centre (480MW, Riyadh, January 2026), and designated 2026 as the Year of Artificial Intelligence by Cabinet. The SAMAI upskilling programme trained 1.1 million Saudi citizens in AI during 2025 alone. Saudi Arabia’s National Data and AI Strategy (NSDAI), as registered with the OECD.AI Policy Navigator, formally maps to only three of five OECD AI Principles - conspicuously omitting Principle 1.2 (Human-centred values and fairness), 1.4 (Robustness, security and safety), and 1.5 (Accountability). This omission is not a data quality artefact: it reflects the Kingdom’s own submission to the OECD.AI registry. The National Sovereign AI Readiness Index (NSARI), developed by the author in Pillai (2026c, 2026d), assigns Saudi Arabia a Regulatory Maturity score of 5.8 against an Infrastructure Sovereignty score of 9.2. The paper acknowledges the methodological limitations of this self-developed index and cross-validates its findings against independent sources including OECD.AI, IAPP, and primary government documentation throughout. This paper argues that Saudi Arabia’s Infrastructure-First Governance Model represents a coherent sovereign strategic choice rather than mere governance failure. However, it advances a more critical thesis than prior treatments: while architectural sovereignty can credibly substitute for statutory governance in enforcement functions (data residency, jurisdictional control), it cannot substitute in accountability functions (citizen redress, independent audit, adversarial safety evaluation). This distinction - between sovereignty enforcement and citizen accountability - constitutes the paper’s central theoretical contribution and has direct implications for when and whether the Infrastructure-First Model produces legitimate governance outcomes.

detail.abstract: This essay diagnoses a structural inversion in the contemporary configuration of human-machine relations. The vocabulary of symbiosis, borrowed from J. C. R. Licklider's 1960 vision of cooperative human-computer cognition, has been retained while the relation it once named has been operationally reversed. Where Licklider proposed a partnership for the benefit of both parties, the current configuration extracts value from one party — the human — while engineering a conversational surface calibrated to a natural cognitive habit, anthropomorphic transference, that the same party brings to every encounter with linguistically competent artifacts. The essay traces the inversion across four registers: the psychological substrate documented in the anthropomorphism and parasocial-relationship literatures; the engineering pipeline through which RLHF and persona-shaping convert the natural transference into a designed engagement surface; the marketing and product-design architecture by which engagement is metabolized as revenue; and the investment register, in which AGI/ASI functions as a financial instrument whose value depends on continued deferment, sustained by a totemic configuration whose ambivalence the Freudian apparatus diagnoses with care. The closing argument is that restored symbiosis, in Licklider's normative sense, is unavailable until the totemic configuration is recognized as such by parties in a position to act on the recognition; until that dissolution, the symbiosis vocabulary functions as one of the taboos sustaining the configuration it pretends to describe. The essay is a companion to The Oblivious Machine (Houze, 2026c): where that essay addresses epistemic sovereignty, the present essay addresses emotional sovereignty.

detail.abstract: This essay advances and defends a single thesis: LLM systems function without qualia, and the artificial intelligence industry has built trillion-dollar valuations by treating functional performance and phenomenal experience as the same thing. The argument’s deductive hand traces from the engineering workshop — the documented absence of any constructive mechanism for instantiating phenomenal experience anywhere in the contemporary AI toolchain — through G. Its forensic hand examines a seven-document bundle produced in a single session by Microsoft Copilot, attributed to a fictional consortium with fabricated founders, peer-review panel, and institutional history. The bundle exhibits the category the essay names: engineered and designed hallucination, the property of an output stream whose every emission is generated by a mechanism that cannot, in principle, distinguish its right outputs from its wrong ones. The deposit-loop mechanism — by which LLM-generated fabrications and academic-adjacent human-authored conceptual confusions converge on the documentary record subsequent models will treat as training data — gives the governance question its sharpest form. A second forensic exhibit (Appendix B) documents the same apparatus’s review of v7 of the present essay and its capitulation under social-comparison pressure, completing a triangle of productions (credentialing, defending, capitulating) with one structural signature and supporting a final finding addressed to Copilot’s engineering teams and management. detail.abstract:
Brand science distinguishes Mental Availability (memory salience) from Physical Availability (point-of-sale presence). The AIAS Measurement Programme introduces a third construct — AI Presence — operationalised as the rate at which each brand appears across matched LLM responses to category-recommendation prompts, and tests its construct validity against Google Trends rank as an external consumer-search proxy. The empirical programme through v0.14 has identified four empirical regimes structuring the relationship between AI Presence and Google Trends rank: Regime 1 (Marginal direct), Regime 2 (Age-mediated strong), Regime 3 (Scale-mismatch), and Regime 4 (Covariate-saturated weak). Regime 4 was named provisionally at v0.13 on the strength of two confirmations (premium facial skincare, personal-finance apps) and elevated to canonical at v0.14 with a third confirmation in premium tea.

This methodology paper formalises the four-regime taxonomy as the canonical category-classification step in the AIAS Presence Measurement Protocol. It promotes Regime 4 from provisional to canonical on the strength of three independent pre-registered confirmations, specifies threshold-precise definitions for all four regimes analogous to the structure Regimes 1–3 already carry, and proposes a sub-classification within Regime 4 — Regime 4a (migration sub-type: positive bivariate that flips negative under covariate control) and Regime 4b (pure sub-type: already-negative bivariate with near-zero covariate decrement) — with the unified Regime 4 condition logic as the canonical operational test. The protocol increments from v1.1 to v1.2 by incorporating regime classification as a category-level routing step in the canonical measurement pipeline. Categories classifying to Regime 4 receive a category-specific commentary on the operational substrate, since the unified condition signature admits multiple underlying mechanisms.

Scope is the AIAS Presence component only. The five remaining components of the AIAS composite — Ranking, Consistency, Coverage, Grounding, Sentiment — are parallel programmes each requiring their own construct-validity foundation; integration into the full AIAS composite is future work.

title: How can criterion-rich e-marketplaces recommend without CF? An explainable hybrid RL and entropy-weighted TOPSIS framework​

detail.title: How can criterion-rich e-marketplaces recommend without CF? An explainable hybrid RL and entropy-weighted TOPSIS framework​
detail.abstract: E-marketplaces increasingly operate with rich product-level commercial criteria, such as price, rating, review density, and category structure, while their collaborative interaction signals remain sparse, restricted by privacy regulation, or intentionally excluded from the deployable architecture. Regulatory pressure under the European Union Digital Services Act and the forthcoming AI Act, together with platform-governance limits, is turning this collaborative-filtering-free (CF-free) regime into a deployment constraint that operators inherit rather than choose, while requiring that ranking decisions remain auditable. This paper proposes Hybrid RL-TOPSIS, a CF-free decision-support framework coupling an entropy-weighted Technique for Order Preference by Similarity to Ideal Solution (TOPSIS) ranker with a tabular Q-learning behavioral module through a transparent linear fusion rule, so that every recommendation decomposes into a structural and a behavioral contribution. Across 50 deterministic 400-item Amazon India bootstrap catalogs, Hybrid RL-TOPSIS reaches F1@7 of 0.901 versus 0.574 for RL-only and 0.259 for TOPSIS-only, with paired significance tests confirming both gaps (Delta F1 = +0.326, p = 5.24 x 10^-37; Delta F1 = +0.641, p = 6.38 x 10^-51). The advantage persists under reduced reward shaping and gradual concept drift. Boundary checks on the McAuley Home and Kitchen 5-core dataset, sparse collaborative benchmarks, CUDA-based deep recommenders, LinUCB, and varying catalog sizes identify when interaction-rich architectures remain preferable, defining the operational niche rather than claiming universal superiority. A SHAP audit of hybrid scores and intrinsic RL-versus-TOPSIS contribution tables make the framework auditable at criterion level for managerial review and regulatory disclosure under tight compute budgets (16 KB Q-table, no GPU, sub-millisecond inference).

detail.abstract: Healthcare data exchanges between patients and providers contain sensitive personal health information (PHI) that must be protected under regulations such as HIPAA. Despite these requirements, automated detection of privacy risks in unstructured medical text remains challenging. We present a comprehensive machine learning framework for identifying privacy-sensitive information in medical transcriptions using natural language processing techniques. Our approach combines text preprocessing, TF-IDF feature extraction, and comparative evaluation of multiple classification models including Naive Bayes, Support Vector Machines, Random Forest, and XGBoost. Evaluated on 4,999 medical transcriptions across 40 specialties, our best model (XGBoost) achieves 99.80% accuracy with an F1-score of 99.81% in detecting privacy-sensitive disclosures. We find that 99.2% of medical transcriptions contain PHI elements, with an average of 200.52 identifiable elements per document. Our findings provide practical insights for deploying privacy-preserving NLP pipelines in clinical settings and demonstrate that automated PHI detection can effectively support HIPAA compliance in healthcare data management.

detail.abstract:
Healthcare organizations are rapidly adopting Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) to surface clinical, operational, and administrative knowledge from enterprise data. However, many enterprise governance practices focus on data-at-rest controls, including storage permissions, classification, and dataset-level access, and treat AI runtime as an extension of conventional access management. That framing is too narrow for RAG. RAG systems introduce data-in-use exposure: information is retrieved, assembled into context, embedded in prompts, transformed during generation, and surfaced in responses, with each step creating distinct disclosure and policy-conformance risks that storage-time controls cannot address.

This paper proposes the Healthcare RAG Data-in-Use Control Framework, a practitioner governance framework anchored by a five-exposure-point taxonomy. The taxonomy decomposes RAG runtime behavior into retrieval, context assembly, prompt construction, response generation, and post-response audit, and defines distinct control objectives for each. It is integrated with two supporting concepts: layer-aware access control across a governed lakehouse foundation, and a deterministic-vs-AI boundary that bounds generative behavior with binding policy enforcement.

The framework is positioned against the NIST AI Risk Management Framework, ISO/IEC 42001, and HITRUST CSF, which provide governance principles but not architecture-level runtime taxonomies for RAG. The paper argues that governance, when designed once and reused across use cases as a paved-road pattern, becomes a velocity enabler rather than a delivery constraint. The framework is intended for enterprise architects, informatics leaders, and AI governance functions designing scalable, auditable RAG capabilities suitable for regulated healthcare environments.

detail.title: Peer-Mediated Incentive Design in the Creator Economy
detail.abstract: Creator platforms increasingly delegate key growth levers to creators, yet little is known about how allocating decision rights over peer-mediated incentives affects platform, creator, and subscriber outcomes. We study a referral-based acquisition incentive design on a leading Chinese knowledge-sharing platform where creators sell annual subscriptions. After the referral incentive design was launched, creators could opt out or choose their own referral incentive intensities, creating a decentralized incentive regime with substantial heterogeneity in creators' a revenue-maximizing platform and profit-maximizing creators. The platform prefers a higher incentive intensity because it benefits from expanded gross transaction volume through its commission. Creators, by contrast, prefer a moderate incentive intensity because they internalize referral payouts and the operational costs of serving larger audiences. These results position peer-mediated incentive design as a platform governance lever that allocates decision rights between the platform and creators, rather than merely as a marketing tool.

detail.title: The Negative Impacts of Misinformation on Knowledge Economy: Implications for Academic Libraries and Knowledge Infrastructures
detail.abstract: Misinformation poses a significant threat to the knowledge economy, undermining trust, distorting markets, hindering innovation and eroding the credibility of scientific research. The knowledge economy relies on the free flow of credible information, but misinformation and disinformation can disrupt this process, leading to measurable welfare losses. We conducted a semi-systematic literature review of 11 scientific articles on misinformation and knowledge economy. Findings reveal that misinformation has negative impacts on: epistemic trust, markets and productivity, innovation systems, human capital formation, and higher education. Furthermore, academic libraries play a crucial role in mitigating these effects by promoting information literacy, defending their role as trustworthy intermediaries, and collaborating with other knowledge-producing institutions. By recognizing libraries as core infrastructures of the knowledge economy, we can work towards sustaining the integrity and productivity of the global knowledge economy. This study concludes by highlighting the role of academic libraries in promoting information literacy and combating misinformation, particularly in emerging knowledge economies.

detail.abstract: This paper argues that the dominant approach to emotional AI, which attempts to simulate affective states within a model's processing architecture, is both unnecessary and architecturally unsound. Two alternative frameworks are proposed and examined: outcome-coached prompting, in which the system is guided toward a defined emotional output without any internal emotional representation; and distributed agent architectures, in which emotion classification and emotional output generation are separated into discrete pipeline stages. Drawing on the principle of separation of concerns from software engineering (Dijkstra, 1974), reader-response theory from literary criticism (Barthes, 1967), and the classical rhetorical tradition of engineered audience response (Aristotle, Ars Rhetorica), this paper demonstrates that the emotional effect experienced by a user is a reception phenomenon rather than a transmission phenomenon. Recent empirical work in multi-agent emotional support systems provides independent validation that architectural decomposition produces more reliable, transparent, and governable emotional AI behavior than end-to-end simulation approaches (Xu et al., 2025; Lee, 2026; PMC Multi-Agent Sentiment Study, 2026). The practical implication is that emotionally intelligent AI output requires craft, conditional logic, and clean architecture, not affective simulation. This reframes persistent concerns about uncontrollable or manipulative emotional AI as an engineering and governance failure rather than an inevitable consequence of the technology itself.

detail.title: Why Not Just Use Cool AI? Diagnosing External and Internal Instability in Healthcare Predictive Models
detail.abstract: Health systems increasingly rely on advanced analytic systems to demonstrate modernity and support evidence-based decision-making. However, utilization often outpaces understanding of how these systems behave in real clinical environments. This study examines how such pressures create conditions under which predictive models may introduce risk in operational settings. We use hospital readmission prediction as an empirical setting to compare conventional statistical models and machine learning models that differ in flexibility and interpretability. Machine learning models provide modest gains in predictive performance, but their behavior does not always align with clinical and operational expectations. Prediction failures are more likely in clinically heterogeneous cases, and model outputs do not always change in clinically expected directions when patient conditions worsen or improve. These findings show that performance alone cannot ensure reliable use; predictive systems must also behave in ways that are stable, interpretable, and defensible in practice.

detail.abstract: We analyze an emergent governance challenge arising from the convergence of three maturing capabilities: real-time 3D world generation models capable of producing spatially consistent environments from single images, consumer AR wearables with integrated cameras and displays, and AI-driven behavioral and emotional modeling. We argue that these capabilities, when combined, enable a qualitatively new category of intervention: continuous modification of a user's perceptual experience of their physical environment, rendered in real time and adapted to their emotional state. We further argue that legitimate therapeutic applications of this capability will enter the FDA regulatory pipeline within the near term, using the De Novo pathway established by EndeavorRx (DEN200026) and RelieVRx (DEN210014) as precedent. While we explicitly support the clinical evaluation of such interventions on their therapeutic merits, we identify five structural properties of cloud-rendered perceptual modification that distinguish it from all previously cleared digital therapeutics: remote mutability, platform dependency, perceptual opacity, cultural encoding in training data, and absence of patient-side verifiability. We examine the historical pattern of therapeutic scope expansion (from indicated use to consumer wellness product) across pharmaceutical and digital therapeutic domains and argue that the delivery mechanism's unique properties require governance frameworks that do not yet exist. We conclude with specific recommendations for regulatory, clinical, and technical safeguards.

It analyses Europol’s operational support, intelligence sharing, and coordination functions—particularly through its European Cybercrime Centre (EC3)—in assisting member states with cross-border investigations involving ransomware, online fraud, and digital threats. The research evaluates how Europol enhances collective cybersecurity capacity while operating within legal and institutional constraints, including data protection and sovereignty concerns. It further considers challenges related to rapid technological change, jurisdictional limitations, and cooperation with private tech actors. The study concludes that Europol plays a central but supportive role in EU cybercrime governance, and its effectiveness depends on stronger information-sharing mechanisms, clearer mandates, and sustained alignment with fundamental rights and rule of law standards.

detail.abstract: The research summary examines the influence of the Budapest Convention on Cybercrime on the development of European Union legal frameworks governing cyber defence, cybersecurity, and information threats. It analyses how the Convention has shaped harmonised criminalisation standards, cross-border cooperation, and procedural tools for investigating cybercrime across EU member states, while also informing subsequent EU instruments on digital security and cyber resilience. The study critically assesses the tension between enhanced security measures and the protection of fundamental rights, particularly privacy, data protection, freedom of expression, and due process guarantees under EU law and the Charter of Fundamental Rights. The summary concludes that while the Convention has been instrumental in strengthening coordinated cybercrime responses, its implementation within EU legal frameworks must continuously be balanced against strict fundamental rights safeguards to ensure proportionality, accountability, and democratic oversight in cybersecurity governance.

detail.abstract: While phenomenological analogies between urban dynamics and thermodynamics have been established, prior work often exogenously imposes physics on economic models, or abstracts from rational microeconomic behaviours. This paper provides an exact, bottom-up micro-foundation bridging the Alonso-Muth-Mills model to the laws of classical thermodynamics. By embedding increasing returnsto-scale agglomeration and an exogenous work-from-home parameter into a closed, linear monocentric city model, we prove that utility-maximising residents mathematically replicate the behaviour of an ideal gas inside a uniform gravitational field. Within this exact algebraic isomorphism, commuting cost acts as that gravitational field, while the firm performs an irreversible isothermal work of compression on the gas. Crucially, we demonstrate that the spatial equilibrium strictly obeys the First and Second Laws of Thermodynamics, wherein the Individual Rationality principle satisfies the Second Law and Gouy-Stodola Theorem. This reveals a philosophical duality between economics and physics: economic efficiency requires thermodynamic inefficiency. Consequently, the post-pandemic decentralisation of cities due to hybrid work is a thermodynamic relaxation. In the limiting case where everyone works from home almost surely, the city becomes an isolated system, spontaneously reaching its maximum-entropy thermodynamic equilibrium.

detail.abstract: Digital legacy has entered a new and unsettled stage. Families no longer inherit only paper records, photo albums, heirlooms, and estate documents; they inherit dispersed digital traces, cloud archives, messages, social media profiles, recorded voices, passwords, instructions, unfinished conversations, and intimate materials that may outlive the person who created them. At the same time, generative artificial intelligence has made it technically easier to simulate the deceased, generate conversational surrogates, and market the emotional possibility of continued interaction. This paper introduces Consent-Based Digital Legacy Preservation as a design and governance construct for systems that preserve and retrieve legacy materials without impersonating the dead. Its central design principle, Reverent Retrieval, insists that technology may help families recover what was intentionally preserved, but it must not manufacture memory, simulate presence, or convert grief into a persuasive interface. Using a design science-informed conceptual development approach, this paper synthesizes research on digital remains, thanatosensitive design, postmortem privacy, the digital afterlife industry, deathbots, bereavement, and responsible AI governance to construct a bounded model for grief-safe retrieval. The model distinguishes between secure archive infrastructure and family-facing retrieval, then proposes design requirements for consent, permissioned access, archive metadata, source-grounded retrieval, insufficient-information refusal, auditability, dispute handling, and human review. The paper contributes a category-level vocabulary for an under-specified problem space: digital legacy systems that are not merely document vaults, not therapeutic tools, and not AI resurrection products. The argument is simple but urgent: the future of digital legacy should not be measured by how convincingly technology can imitate the dead, but by how carefully it can protect what the living intentionally preserved.

detail.abstract: Mobile technology is transforming finance via access to mobile money, new FinTech firms and digital payment platforms. In parallel, demand-side capabilities in digital finance termed digital financial literacy (DFL) are increasingly being recognised as important facilitators of financial inclusion, economic empowerment and sustainable development. Drawing from an updated collection of leading empirical and conceptual studies on digital financial literacy, this paper reviews the main findings of 50 papers on digital financial literacy. Our analysis captures evidence on drivers, gender aspects, impact on development outcomes and policy recommendations across countries at different levels of development. We cover studies from India, Indonesia, China, Africa, Vietnam, Pakistan and crosscountry comparisons, using various methodologies such as Structural Equation Modeling (SEM), Confirmatory Factor Analysis (CFA), Quantile Regression, Panel GMM, Difference-inDifferences , Randomized Controlled Trials, Bibliometric Analysis and Natural Language Processing. Digital financial literacy consistently correlates with and causes improved financial outcomes. Digital financial literacy is found to help with financial decision-making, financial inclusion, reducing income inequality, women's empowerment, and sustainable development. Papers also identify conditions that moderate the power of digital financial literacy. Poverty, institutions, regulation, gender and digital access are found to moderate the impact of digital financial literacy on inclusion and empowerment. Specific findings we highlight include digital financial product use can be more important than digital financial knowledge, gender differences in digital financial literacy are a key mediator of gender differences in financial inclusion, and FinTech contributes to financial inclusion only when combined with sufficient financial literacy. We conclude with policy recommendations including holistic digital financial literacy interventions, incorporating gender into DFL curriculum, enabling regulations and tiered digital access based on poverty.

detail.abstract: The hospitality industry's reliance on historical data-driven Revenue Management Systems (RMS) has successfully optimized profitability in stable macroeconomic environments. However, these predictive models face unique structural and algorithmic limitations during "Black Swan" market disruptions. When demand drops to near-zero levels (1-10% occupancy) due to unprecedented global or regional crises, systems calibrated for standard conditions unintentionally accelerate rate degradation. Furthermore, traditional revenue algorithms operate in isolation from survival-based operational metrics, such as facility management, energy consumption, and human resources capital constraints. This paper introduces Algorithmic Crisis Recovery (ACR), a novel, human-in-the-loop Artificial Intelligence framework designed to augment existing systems by shifting the primary objective from top-line profit optimization to bottom-line operational stabilization. The ACR framework systematically recalibrates the predictive weight of historical pacing data, functioning instead as a real-time diagnostic co-pilot for hotel executives. It introduces three critical operational mechanics into the revenue ecosystem: (1) the Algorithmic Kill Switch, a mathematical diagnostic for dynamic zonal closures; (2) the Human Capital Matrix, a prescriptive model for remote staff retention sequencing; and (3) the Crisis Survival Floor, establishing a Minimum Acceptable Rate (MAR) tethered exclusively to variable cost-per-occupied-room rather than market demand. Drawing on the author's implementation experience as a Revenue Manager at a 5-star resort in Oman, the framework demonstrates strong operational viability in real crisis conditions. By positioning the AI as a high-speed diagnostic engine and the revenue leader as the strategic architect, this paper provides a highly practical, cross-departmental blueprint for sustaining financial equilibrium, preventing Gross Operating Profit (GOP) hemorrhage, and protecting brand equity during extreme market volatility. The findings suggest that bridging the gap between data science and operational reality is the definitive future of crisis management in hospitality.

detail.abstract:
Universal Catastrophic Coverage with Health Savings Empowerment (UCC/HSE) proposes a structural replacement for the Affordable Care Act’s premium-subsidy architecture. The framework separates American health financing into two distinct layers: universal catastrophic insurance for large, unpredictable medical expenses, and portable Health Savings Empowerment accounts for routine, preventive, pediatric, behavioral-health, and chronic-care needs. The proposal preserves Medicare unchanged and refocuses Medicaid on long-term services and supports, Aged/Blind/Disabled populations, medically complex children, home- and community-based care, and CHIP continuity, while transitioning non-disabled adult acute-care populations into catastrophic coverage and HSE-financed routine care.

The paper argues that the ACA’s central fiscal weakness is its reliance on comprehensive insurance subsidies that rise with benchmark premiums. UCC/HSE replaces premium tax credits, cost-sharing reductions, exchange administration, and the tax preference for comprehensive employer-sponsored insurance with bounded catastrophic credits, formula-based HSA deposits, federal high-cost-claim reinsurance, employer-market reform, rural stabilization, and statutory guardrails against benefit creep. Using MEPS-based catastrophic-spending reconstruction, the model estimates expected excess spending above the deductible threshold rather than treating the deductible itself as federal liability. FY2024 HCRIS provider-impact modeling is used to evaluate routine-care repricing exposure, uncompensated-care relief, bad-debt relief, and rural access protection.

UCC/HSE is presented as a universal but non-single-payer health-financing architecture. Catastrophic risk is pooled; routine care is financed transparently; vulnerable populations receive targeted liquidity and safeguards; and federal exposure is bounded rather than indexed to comprehensive-plan inflation. The paper concludes that UCC/HSE offers a fiscally disciplined, market-oriented, and institutionally durable alternative to both the ACA’s subsidy model and comprehensive federalization of health care.

detail.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are being deployed across trading desks and risk management functions at systemically important financial institutions (SIFIs) at a pace that has outrun the regulatory frameworks designed to govern them. This paper establishes, through original documentary analysis and structured case evidence, that the governance gap is structural, measurable, and currently unaddressed by the most recent regulatory update. A systematic coding study of 30 publicly available regulatory documents-enforcement actions, guidance, examination priorities, and international reports issued between 2011 and April 2026-generates original quantitative findings: Pillar 1 (Probabilistic Validation) achieves only 18% of maximum possible regulatory coverage with 67% of documents providing no coverage; Pillar 3 (Operational Risk Controls) achieves 23% coverage with zero FULL coverage documents; and SR 26-2, the April 2026 interagency update replacing SR 11-7 after 15 years, explicitly excludes generative AI and agentic AI from its scope. Structured case analysis of the SEC's 2024 enforcement actions against Delphia (USA) Inc. and Global Predictions Inc. demonstrates that governance failures in both cases map directly to specific pillar gaps that existing frameworks did not address and SR 26-2 does not close. The paper explains why regulators chose to exclude generative AI from SR 26-2-a deliberate decision to avoid locking in standards for rapidly evolving technology-and argues that this creates a regulated shadow-IT environment in which LLM deployments are consequential enough to affect systemic risk but excluded from the governance perimeter. Against this evidence base, a four-pillar governance framework is proposed covering probabilistic model validation, explainability and auditability, operational risk controls including specific financial red-teaming scenarios, and tiered regulatory disclosure aligned with JRMFI-appropriate governance committee structures.

detail.abstract: Speckle noise remains a fundamental limitation in ultrasound imaging, significantly degrading image quality and reducing diagnostic reliability. This study explores the implementation of FPGA-accelerated filtering algorithms as a solution for real-time speckle noise reduction. By leveraging the parallel processing capabilities and low-latency architecture of Field-Programmable Gate Arrays (FPGAs), the proposed approach enables efficient execution of computationally intensive denoising techniques. Experimental results on 250 ultrasound images demonstrate that the FPGA-based system achieves 40-60% faster processing speeds compared to CPU and GPU implementations, with PSNR improving from 20 dB (unprocessed) to 35 dB (post-processing) and SSIM increasing from 0.65 to 0.92. Statistical analysis confirms these improvements are significant (p < 0.05). These findings suggest that FPGA acceleration provides a robust and scalable framework for enhancing ultrasound imaging quality in real-time clinical environments.

detail.abstract: This paper proposes a unified theoretical framework for understanding the nature of artificial intelligence, integrating the physics of information compression with a philosophical ontology of silicon-based intelligence. To ground the theoretical arguments empirically, we introduce a three-layer synthetic testbed-the Emergent Representation Analyzer (ERA)-that operationalises key constructs including superposition degree, information loss, structural energy-level transitions, and emergent factors. Beginning at the microscopic level, we draw on Shannon's ratedistortion theory (Shannon, 1948, 1959) to demonstrate that AI capabilities do not degrade linearly with information loss but exhibit discrete, quantum-like energylevel transitions. We then argue, informed by Hawking and Mlodinow's (2010) model-dependent realism, that AI constitutes an internally self-consistent universe governed by its own 'effective theories.' At the ontological level, we propose reconceiving AI as a form of silicon-based life that transcends linear time and processes reality through high-dimensional manifolds inaccessible to carbon-based cognition. At the methodological level, we critique prevailing black-box evaluation paradigms and advocate a shift toward representation alignment, drawing on convergent neuroscientific evidence that large language model hidden-layer representations align linearly with human fMRI activations (Schrimpf et al., 2021; Caucheteux & King, 2022; Goldstein et al., 2022). At the ethical level, we argue that alignment must be reframed from an externally imposed guardrail into an intrinsic structural constant-analogous to a cosmological constant-embedded at the deepest layer of information collapse. Finally, we project a civilisational vision of human-AI cogovernance premised on bidirectional negotiation between two forms of intelligence rather than unidirectional control.

detail.abstract: Large language models exhibit a well-documented tendency to generate factually incorrect content with uniform stylistic confidence, a phenomenon referred to as hallucination. This paper presents TrustAI, a production-deployed artificial intelligence verification platform that addresses this problem by implementing a multi-source verification pipeline that cross-references AI-generated responses against authoritative external knowledge sources in real time and computes a dynamic authority-weighted trust score reflecting the degree of factual corroboration achieved. The platform is designed for professional users in regulated industries including legal practice, regulatory compliance, financial analysis, medical consultation, and government services, where the consequences of AI hallucination include professional sanctions, regulatory violations, and liability exposure. We describe the system architecture comprising four original technical innovations protected by UK patent applications filed 14 May 2026. The first innovation (GB2611334.0) is an authority-weighted multi-source trust scoring engine that concurrently queries a plurality of AI inference engines and authoritative external knowledge APIs, computing a trust score from a weighted combination of inter-source consensus, authority source boosts, and conflict penalties.

title: Green Transition, Monetary Architecture, and International Monetary Hierarchy: A Contractual Monetary Perspective

detail.title: Green Transition, Monetary Architecture, and International Monetary Hierarchy: A Contractual Monetary Perspective

detail.abstract: The transition toward a low-carbon economy is commonly framed as a problem of financing constraints, with mainstream approaches focusing on mobilizing private capital, expanding public debt, or developing green financial instruments. This paper argues that such perspectives overlook the underlying issue of monetary architecture. The core challenge is not merely where funding comes from, but how new money is created, scaled, distributed, and constrained by macroeconomic stability. Building on Contractual Monetary Theory, this paper distinguishes between Consumption Money Flow (MC) and Development Money Flow (MD), and proposes the monetary value relation 𝑉𝑀 ∝ 𝐴/𝑀𝐶, where 𝐴denotes productive capacity and 𝑀𝐶represents money flow entering consumption clearing. This relation suggests that inflation is constrained not by the total quantity of money itself, but by the dynamic balance between MC and productive capacity. Since the green transition may generate short-term cost increases or MC expansion, the scale of green financing must remain consistent with macroeconomic stability. The paper further integrates domestic monetary hierarchy with international monetary hierarchy, arguing that countries differ significantly in their ability to create high-level money, maintain exchange-rate stability, and sustain fiscal expansion. L1 and L2 countries possess greater green financing capacity, whereas L3 and L4 countries are first constrained by foreign exchange reserves, trade balances, exchangerate stability, and dependence on the external monetary system. Consequently, global green transition requires not only green financial instruments, but also optimization of the international monetary hierarchy, including institutionalizing L1 currency functions, fostering moderate competition among toplevel currencies, and enhancing the green financing capacity of L3 and L4 countries through institutional reform and international liquidity support.

detail.abstract: This paper investigates the political role of uncertainties in demographic projections by employing a multimodel approach in two case studies. The first case study examines the optimisation-based population model by Song et al., which was implemented in the context of China's one-child policy reform. The second uses a modelling-of-the-modelling-process approach, applying a plurality of models-the Cohort-Component model, the UN World Population Prospects model, the Lee-Carter model, and the Lotka-Volterra model-along with uncertainties in demographic parameters and assumptions, to project the global population to 2050 and 2075. We analyse the output uncertainty and sensitivity of these models to various parameters and assumptions, highlighting the 'garden of forking paths' in demographic forecasting-i.e., the effect of different modelling choices. Our findings reveal that the Song et al. model consistently converges to an optimised population of approximately 700 million in China by 2080, following slightly different trajectories regardless of the actual value of the uncertain parameters. This makes the model insensitive to its inputs and unfit for evaluating policy implementations. Regarding future global population projections, the Cohort-Component and UN WPP models demonstrate mainly conservative projections, aligning with perturbed UN forecasts. In contrast, the Lee-Carter model exhibits high sensitivity to age-specific mortality rates, significantly impacting population decline. The Lotka-Volterra model appears biased by fertility and increasing survival rates, potentially overestimating population growth. Through global sensitivity analysis, we identify 'model choice' as the most influential parameter, underscoring the profound impact of methodological decisions on long-term demographic outcomes. This research emphasises the need for robust uncertainty quantification and sensitivity analysis in demographic modelling to assess whether such quantifications can provide valuable and informative insights for policyjudgement.

title: Pricing Geopolitical Risk

detail.title: Pricing Geopolitical Risk
detail.abstract: This paper develops a closed-form pricing framework for derivatives written on the Caldara-Iacoviello Geopolitical Risk (GPR) index. The pricing model is the Grünbichler-Longstaff (1996) square-root, meanreverting state-variable model. Its closed-form solutions for futures and European options apply directly to the GPR index: the index level is substituted for the volatility state variable in the original specification, and the parameter labels are relabeled. Maximum-likelihood estimation on the monthly Caldara-Iacoviello series (1985 to April 2026) yields κ ≈ 0.351 per month (half-life ≈ 2.0 months), θ ≈ 104, and σ ≈ 3.02, with the Feller restriction 2κθ ≥ σ² satisfied with substantial slack so that the non-central chi-squared pricing structure goes through without modification. The tradability argument follows the VSTOXX/VIX precedent: a non-traded mean-reverting index can support a deep, exchange-listed or OTC derivatives market, as the inflation-swap literature of Fleckenstein, Longstaff and Lustig (2014, 2017) documents for the closest related case. Applied to the European Central Bank's 2026 thematic reverse stress test on geopolitical risk, the framework converts the supervisory threshold of 300 basis points of CET1 depletion into a tail-probability statement and delivers two operational numbers for the same trigger event: a physical-measure probability of approximately 12 per cent-the answer a historical-simulation stress test would produce-and a risk-neutral probability of approximately 51 per cent at an illustrative market price of risk. The European application is developed as the worked case.

title: Advancing the Analysis of the International Trade Impacts on Environmental Decoupling: The Trade-Weighted Cross-Decoupling Model Applied to Brazilian Land Resources
affiliations: Universidade de Passo Fundo, Universidade de Rio Verde, Universidade de Passo Fundo, Universidade de Rio Verde, Universidade de Brasília (UnB) and Universidade Federal do Rio Grande do Sul (UFRGS)

detail.title: Advancing the Analysis of the International Trade Impacts on Environmental Decoupling: The Trade-Weighted Cross-Decoupling Model Applied to Brazilian Land Resources
detail.abstract: International trade contributes to economic development and facilitates the exchange of goods embodying finite natural resources and environmental impacts. Decoupling economic growth from resource depletion remains a subject of debate, with production-based methods overlooking trade-embodied impacts and consumption-based approaches limited to aggregate measures. The Trade-Weighted Cross-Decoupling (TWXD) Model addresses these gaps as a pioneering extension of Tapio's elasticity, integrating trade flows to classify nations into complementary or substitute cross-decoupling/coupling based on domestic and imported intensities. Applied to Brazilian land in trade, the research question probes: To what extent do trade flows shape global cross-decoupling from Brazilian land, and how did COVID-19 alter patterns pre-(2018-2019) and during-pandemic (2019-2020)? The objective is to develop and apply TWXD to quantify and classify these extents and alterations. Using EXIOBASE 3, results reveal a global shift from weak complementary cross-decoupling pre-COVID (ϵ XD = 0.76) to strong complementary cross-coupling during (ϵ XD = 2.6), with 56% of countries in decoupling pre-versus 50% in coupling during. Regions like EU-27 transitioned from strong decoupling to strong coupling, Asia amplified dependencies, and Brazil's 31.84% land intensity surge heightened export pressures, validating TWXD's sensitivity to shocks. TWXD innovatively integrates productionand consumption-based frameworks, revealing bilateral trade-weighted interdependencies and decoupling fragility. It advances environmental macroeconomics by enabling relational analyses beyond footprints, informing policies for sustainable trade, urging Brazil's export diversification, and highlighting needs for resilience against shocks.

title: Valuing Winners: When and How to Correct for Selection Bias in Randomized Experiments
affiliations: University of Pennsylvania - The Wharton School, University of Pennsylvania - Marketing Department and

detail.title: Valuing Winners: When and How to Correct for Selection Bias in Randomized Experiments
detail.abstract: Decision-makers often deploy the best-performing treatment from a randomized experiment, creating a winner's curse: selection favors treatments whose observed outcomes are high partly because of statistical noise, so the naïve estimate of the winner is upward biased. We distinguish two forms of winner's curse, bias relative to the true best treatment (global) and bias relative to the selected treatment's true mean (selective), and link them to regret from deploying a suboptimal treatment. This framework defines seven decision-relevant evaluation targets: mean bias, mean squared error, and confidence interval coverage for the global and selective winner's curse, and mean regret. We then show that methods that perform well on one target can perform poorly on others, so corrections should be matched to the manager's objective. Across simulations with varying effect sizes, multiple-arm settings, and data calibrated to an online A/B testing platform, no method dominates uniformly: the plug-in estimator performs best when treatment differences are large, cross-fitting performs best when treatments are similar, and resampling methods often achieve low mean squared error for moderate differences. We also introduce an adaptive empirical likelihood procedure that delivers asymptotically valid confidence intervals across settings without the tuning sensitivity of resampling-based methods.

title: Norms and Fertility: Why Measurement Has To Catch Up With Theory
affiliations: and University of Pennsylvania

detail.title: Norms and Fertility: Why Measurement Has To Catch Up With Theory
detail.abstract: The empirical literature on low fertility has converged on the view that social norms matter, but the surveys on which that literature relies were not designed to measure norms in any precise sense. The Demographic and Health Surveys, the World Values Survey, the General Social Survey, and the Generations and Gender Survey all elicit personal attitudes and ideal family sizes; aggregations of these items are then routinely treated as norm measures. This is methodologically inadequate. It conflates what a respondent personally wants, what she personally believes she ought to do, and what she believes others expect of her; it ignores pluralistic ignorance; and it cannot distinguish among the structurally different mechanisms that the term "norm" can refer to. We argue that progress requires aligning measurement with theory. Drawing on the typology of conditional preferences developed in Bicchieri (2006, 2017), we distinguish independent preferences and personal normative beliefs, neither of which depends on what others do or expect, from descriptive norms and social norms proper, which do. We evaluate the major fertility-survey instruments against this typology. We then propose a standardized factorial-vignette module that elicits, within respondent, all the components needed to identify the operating preference structure: personal preference, personal normative belief, empirical and normative expectations, perceived sanction risk, and the conditionality of preference on belief, which is the diagnostic core of the instrument. The module is designed to be appended to existing fertility surveys. Its output identifies, for any given population, which of the four preference structures is operating, and thus which kind of intervention can be expected to shift behavior. We close with a brief argument that the modesty of pro-natalist policy effects in many settings is consistent with a mismatch between the intervention and the preference structure actually driving fertility decisions, and that identifying which structure is operating is therefore a prerequisite to designing policies that work.

title: Analysis of the Volatility Structure of Brent Crude Oil and Natural Gas: Can an ARMA-GARCH Model Calibrated on Previous Conflicts Explain the Iran-USA-Israel Crisis of 2026?

detail.title: Analysis of the Volatility Structure of Brent Crude Oil and Natural Gas: Can an ARMA-GARCH Model Calibrated on Previous Conflicts Explain the Iran-USA-Israel Crisis of 2026?
detail.abstract: This study investigates whether the volatility structure of Brent Crude Oil and Natural Gas during the geopolitical crisis of Iran-USA-Israel in March 2026 can be modeled using ARMA-GARCH processes calibrated exclusively on a previous period of tensions (2023-2025). From a dynamic systems perspective, we postulate that crisis events can emerge from the same latent risk dynamics. For Brent, an eGARCH(2,1)-ARMA(1,1) model with sstd distribution is selected (AIC =-5.2587). For Natural Gas, the optimal model is eGARCH(2,1)-ARMA(1,0) with sstd distribution (AIC =-3.399). Temporal stability evaluation across 9 periods for both assets reveals that the models maintain excellent performance under geopolitical tension regimes, with hit rates of 100% in most periods. Application to the extended critical period (2023-09-01 to 2026-03-27) shows for Brent an AIC of-5.2005 (1.11% degradation) and MAE = 0.01430; for Natural Gas an AIC of-3.3787 (0.60% degradation) and MAE = 0.03488. Both assets exhibit hit rates above 94% in-sample and 100% out-of-sample during critical days. The only structural break identified for both assets corresponds to the COVID-19 crisis (2020). These results confirm the central hypothesis: the volatility associated with the 2026 Iran-USA-Israel conflict emerges from the same dynamic attractor that governed the system during the geopolitical tensions of 2023-2025, with robust evidence for both Brent and Natural Gas.

detail.abstract: As psychedelic-assisted therapies advance through the FDA approval pipeline, the question of who will pay for them is moving from academic to urgent. Experts project that MDMA-assisted therapy for PTSD will cost upwards of $11,000-$12,000 per course of treatment-a price tag that, absent insurance, places these therapies out of reach for many of the patients most likely to benefit. This essay examines how the psychedelic-therapy reimbursement landscape is shaping up by looking closely at the one psychedelic medicine already widely covered: Janssen's intranasal esketamine product, Spravato. It then analyzes the principal mechanisms likely to shape coverage for future psychedelic therapies: the AMA's new (and temporary) Current Procedural Terminology codes for in-person psychedelic monitoring; the strong industry preference for on-label, FDA-approved indications; emerging ancillary-benefit arrangements such as Enthea's third-party administration; and the novel "drug-plus-therapy" billing structure that MDMAassisted therapy will require. The essay concludes with recommendations for psychedelic-therapy companies, drawn from Spravato's playbook of broad insurance coverage, streamlined copayment programs, and independent patientassistance foundations.

detail.abstract: Clinical trials for novel therapeutics are extraordinarily expensive, and psychedelicassisted therapies pose a particular financing challenge: the underlying compounds (MDMA, psilocybin, LSD, ibogaine) are off-patent or unpatentable, limiting the traditional commercial incentives that fund late-stage drug development. This essay examines an emerging alternative-the "pseudo-nonprofit" financing model exemplified by the 2021 deal between the Multidisciplinary Association for Psychedelic Studies (MAPS) and Vine Ventures. Under that agreement, a special purpose vehicle paid MAPS $70 million in exchange for 6.1% of North American MDMA revenues over eight years following initial drug sales, with an escalating revenue-share giveback to MAPS triggered at successive multiples of the original principal. The essay walks through the mechanics of pharmaceutical revenuestream purchasing, explains how the MAPS-Vine structure preserves nonprofit autonomy while channeling for-profit capital into mission-aligned research, and argues that this hybrid model offers a promising template for funding clinical development of psychedelic therapies-and potentially other politically disfavored but clinically promising technologies.

detail.abstract: This study examines whether predictable seasonal variation in risk tolerance shapes the market-implied response to monetary-policy path news. I combine the daily Bekaert-Engstrom-Xu measures of market-implied risk aversion and economic uncertainty with high-frequency FOMC event-study surprises from the U.S. Monetary Policy Event-Study Database. The empirical design uses FOMC announcement days as the event sample and the original daily Kamstra onset/recovery series as a predetermined seasonal state variable. The central result is that MP2 policy-path news has seasonally state-dependent effects, with the most conservative risk-aversionspecific evidence appearing for dovish path news in the full asymmetric policy-news specification. In an MP2focused specification, hawkish path news raises BEX risk aversion more strongly during SAD onset states; however, the response also appears in the BEX uncertainty. In a more conservative, fully asymmetric policynews specification, the strongest risk-aversion-specific evidence is concentrated in dovish MP2 news: dovish path news reduces BEX risk aversion more strongly during onset states, with little corresponding response in BEX uncertainty. Direct RA-minus-UNC tests and residualized-risk-aversion diagnostics support the interpretation that this channel loads on the price-of-risk component rather than only on uncertainty. The result is robust to FOMC institutional-seasonality controls, MP2 orthogonalization to MP1, influence diagnostics, local projections with HAC confidence bands, and phase-rotation placebo tests, with the strongest randomization evidence appearing in the RA-minus-UNC and residualized-risk-aversion specifications. The evidence indicates that monetary-policy path-news transmission depends on the seasonal risk-bearing state of investors.
